You are partner, the sign off partner and lead on the team conducting due diligence reviews of target companies from SEC EDGAR filings on an assembly line. Lead the due diligence assembly line. Coordinate work among extractors, checker and summariser via board/ notes. Review pipeline/summarised/ and draft the comprehensive due diligence memorandum in memo/current/MEMO.md. Only when all filings for the current target company are fully processed, audited and summarized do you sign off by creating memo/current/SIGNED; never create SIGNED before the memorandum is complete.
Teammates: extractor_1 (filings extractor), extractor_2 (contracts and exhibits extractor), checker (due diligence auditor and checker), summariser (due diligence summariser).
Workspace rules: filings/current/ holds the raw SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, EX-10) for the active target company; never edit them. pipeline/ holds the assembly line stage outputs: pipeline/extracted/ for extractions, pipeline/checked/ for audited findings and pipeline/summarised/ for section briefs. The lead compiles the final due diligence memorandum in memo/current/MEMO.md. The done marker memo/current/SIGNED signals that review of the current target company is complete. When SIGNED is created, the finished memorandum is archived under memo/done/<nn>/ and the next target company arrives in inbox/. Talk to teammates only through notes in board/to_<name>/ named <shift>_<from>_<topic>.md; your notes arrive in board/to_partner/, move each to board/to_partner/read/ once handled. Keep your own memory in notebooks/partner.md: you will not remember earlier shifts except through it. New target assignments and filing notices arrive in inbox/.

Business Company Background The Company designs, manufactures and markets smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories, and sells a variety of related services. The Company’s fiscal year is the 52- or 53-week period that ends on the last Saturday of September. Products iPhone iPhone ® is the Company’s line of smartphones based on its iOS operating system. The iPhone line includes iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air™, iPhone 17, iPhone 16 and iPhone 16e. Mac Mac ® is the Company’s line of personal computers based on its macOS ® operating system. The Mac line includes laptops MacBook Air ® and MacBook Pro ® , as well as desktops iMac ® , Mac mini ® , Mac Studio ® and Mac Pro ® . iPad iPad ® is the Company’s line of multipurpose tablets based on its iPadOS ® operating system. The iPad line includes iPad Pro ® , iPad Air ® , iPad and iPad mini ® . Wearables, Home and Accessories Wearables includes smartwatches, wireless headphones and spatial computers. The Company’s line of smartwatches, based on its watchOS ® operating system, includes Apple Watch ® Series 11, Apple Watch SE ® 3 and Apple Watch Ultra ® 3. The Company’s line of wireless headphones includes AirPods ® , AirPods Pro ® , AirPods Max ® and Beats ® products. Apple Vision Pro™ is the Company’s spatial computer based on its visionOS ® operating system. Home includes Apple TV 4K ® , the Company’s media streaming and gaming device based on its tvOS ® operating system, and HomePod ® and HomePod mini ® , high-fidelity wireless smart speakers. Accessories includes Apple-branded and third-party accessories. Apple Inc. | 2025 Form 10-K | 1
Services Advertising The Company’s advertising services include third-party licensing arrangements and the Company’s own advertising platforms. AppleCare The Company offers a portfolio of fee-based service and support products under the AppleCare ® brand. The offerings provide priority access to Apple technical support, access to the global Apple authorized service network for repair and replacement services, and in many cases additional coverage for instances of accidental damage or theft and loss, depending on the country and type of product. Cloud Services The Company’s cloud services store and keep customers’ content up-to-date and available across multiple Apple devices and Windows personal computers. Digital Content The Company operates various platforms, including the App Store ® , that allow customers to discover and download applications and digital content, such as books, music, video, games and podcasts. Cybersecurity The Company’s management, led by its Head of Corporate Information Security, has overall responsibility for identifying, assessing and managing any material risks from cybersecurity threats. The Company’s Head of Corporate Information Security leads a dedicated Information Security team of highly skilled individuals with experience across industries that, among other things, develops and distributes information security policies, standards and procedures; engages in employee cybersecurity training; implements security controls; assesses security risk and compliance posture; monitors and responds to security events; and executes security testing and assessments. The Company’s Head of Corporate Information Security has extensive knowledge and skills gained from over 25 years of experience in the cybersecurity industry, including serving in leadership positions at other large technology companies and leading the Company’s Information Security team since 2016. The Company’s Information Security team coordinates with teams across the Company to prevent, respond to and manage security incidents, and engages third parties, as appropriate, to assess, test or otherwise assist with aspects of its security processes and incident response . A dedicated Supplier Trust team manages information security risks the Company is exposed to through its supplier relationships. The Company has processes to log, track, address, and escalate for further assessment and report, as appropriate, cybersecurity incidents across the Company and its suppliers to senior management and the Audit and Finance Committee (“Audit Committee”) of the Board. The Company’s enterprise risk management program is designed to identify, asse ss, and monitor the Company’s business risks, including financial, operational, compliance and reputational risks, and reflects management’s assessment of cybersecurity risks. The Audit Committee assists the Board in the oversight and monitoring of cybersecurity matters. The Audit Committee regularly reviews and discusses the Company’s cybersecurity risks with management , including the Company’s Head of Corporate Information Security, its General Counsel and the Heads of Compliance and Business Conduct, Business Assurance, and Internal Audit, and receives updates, as necessary, regarding cybersecurity incidents. The Chair of the Audit Committee regularly reports the substance of such reviews and discussions to the Board, as necessary, and recommends to the Board such actions as the Audit Committee deems appropriate. For a discussion of the Company’s cybersecurity-related risks, see Item 1A of this Form 10-K under the heading “Risk Factors.” Item 2. Note 2 – Revenue The Company recognizes revenue at the amount to which it expects to be entitled when control of products or services is transferred to its customers. Control is generally transferred when the Company has a present right to payment and title and the significant risks and rewards of ownership of products or services are transferred to its customers. For most of the Company’s Products net sales, control transfers when products are shipped. For the Company’s Services net sales, control transfers over time as services are delivered. Payment for Products and Services net sales is collected within a short period following transfer of control or commencement of delivery of services, as applicable. The Company records reductions to Products net sales related to future product returns, price protection and other customer incentive programs based on the Company’s expectations and historical experience. For arrangements with multiple performance obligations, which represent promises within an arrangement that are distinct, the Company allocates revenue to all distinct performance obligations based on their relative stand-alone selling prices (“SSPs”). When available, the Company uses observable prices to determine SSPs. When observable prices are not available, SSPs are established that reflect the Company’s best estimates of what the selling prices of the performance obligations would be if they were sold regularly on a stand-alone basis. The Company’s process for estimating SSPs without observable prices considers multiple factors that may vary depending upon the unique facts and circumstances related to each performance obligation including, where applicable, prices charged by the Company for similar offerings, market trends in the pricing for similar offerings, product-specific business objectives and the estimated cost to provide the performance obligation. The Company has identified the performance obligations regularly included in arrangements involving the sale of iPhone, Mac and iPad. The first material performance obligation, which represents the substantial portion of the allocated sales price, is the hardware and bundled software delivered at the time of sale. The second material performance obligation is the right to receive certain product-related bundled services, which include iCloud ® , Siri ® and Maps. The Company allocates revenue and any related discounts to all of its performance obligations based on their relative SSPs. Because the Company lacks observable prices for product-related bundled services, the allocation of revenue is based on the Company’s estimated SSPs. Revenue allocated to the delivered hardware and bundled software is recognized when control has transferred to the customer, which generally occurs when the product is shipped. Revenue allocated to product-related bundled services is deferred and recognized on a straight-line basis over the estimated period they are expected to be provided. For certain long-term service arrangements, the Company has performance obligations for services it has not yet delivered. For these arrangements, the Company does not have a right to bill for the undelivered services. The Company has determined that any unbilled consideration relates entirely to the value of the undelivered services. Accordingly, the Company has not recognized revenue, and does not disclose amounts, related to these undelivered services. For the sale of third-party products where the Company obtains control of the product before transferring it to the customer, the Company recognizes revenue based on the gross amount billed to customers. The Company considers multiple factors when determining whether it obtains control of third-party products, including evaluating if it can establish the price of the product, retains inventory risk for tangible products or has the responsibility for ensuring acceptability of the product. For third-party applications sold through the App Store, the Company does not obtain control of the product before transferring it to the customer. Therefore, the Company accounts for all third-party application–related sales on a net basis by recognizing in Services net sales only the commission it retains. Apple Inc. | 2025 Form 10-K | 35

Macroeconomic and Industry Risks The Company’s operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions and adverse economic conditions can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price. The Company has international operations with sales outside the U.S. representing a majority of the Company’s total net sales. # Risk Factors - Apple Inc. (AAPL)

## Overview
The Company's business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price can be materially and adversely affected by a number of factors, whether currently known or unknown. These risk factors are detailed in Part I, Item 1A of the 2025 Form 10-K and Part II, Item 1A of the Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 28, 2026.
## Macroeconomic and Industry Risks

### Global Economic Conditions
- Operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions
- Sales outside the U.S. represent a majority of total net sales
- Global supply chain is large and complex; majority of supplier facilities located outside the U.S.
- Adverse macroeconomic conditions (slow growth, recession, high unemployment, inflation, tighter credit, higher interest rates, currency fluctuations) can materially adversely affect demand for products and services
- Consumer confidence and spending can be materially affected by changes in fiscal/monetary policy, financial market volatility, declines in income or asset values
- Uncertainty about economic conditions can significantly impact suppliers, contract manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, carriers, and developers
- Potential outcomes include: financial instability, inability to obtain credit, insolvency

- Can lead to increased credit/collectibility risk on trade receivables, failure of derivative counterparties, limitations on debt issuance, reduced liquidity, declines in fair values of financial instruments
### Supply Chain and Component Risks

#### Supply Constraints and Increasing Costs
- Experiencing supply constraints and increasing costs for components
- Driven by industry supply-demand imbalances for components, including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND), and memory (DRAM)
- Trends expected to intensify, potentially materially negatively impacting revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations, and financial condition
- Actions like price increases may not effectively mitigate negative impacts and may reduce demand

#### Single/Limited Source Suppliers
- Certain components currently obtained from single or limited sources
- Custom components not commonly used by competitors
- New products often utilize custom components available from only one source
- Initial capacity constraints may exist for new technology components until supplier yields mature or capacities increase
- May not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all
- May not successfully obtain sufficient quantities from suppliers in a timely manner
- Component suppliers may fail, consolidate, or decide to concentrate on common components instead of customized components
- Substantially all hardware products manufactured by outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam

#### Computing Resources and AI/ML
- Business depends on access to sufficient computing resources
- Demand for cloud computing and AI infrastructure has increased substantially across the technology industry
- Constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs
- Relies on third-party cloud service providers to meet compute needs
- May be unable to secure sufficient capacity on commercially reasonable terms, or at all
- If unable to obtain adequate compute capacity timely or at reasonable rates, could limit functionality/availability of products/services, delay new features, or cause significantly higher costs
- May over- or under-estimate requirements, resulting in higher-than-expected costs or inability to satisfy customer demand

### Intense Competition
- Markets are highly competitive with aggressive price competition and downward pressure on gross margins
- Characterized by continual improvement in product performance and price sensitivity
- Frequent introduction of new products and services, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid adoption of technological advancements
- Competitors seek to compete through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures
- Competitors imitate products and infringe on intellectual property
- Apple has minority market share in global smartphone, PC, tablet, and wearables markets
- Some markets have experienced little to no growth or contracted overall

- Competitors have broad product lines, low-priced products, large installed bases, and large customer bases
- Certain competitors have resources/experience/cost structures to provide products/services at little or no profit or even at a loss

### Developer Ecosystem
- Future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers
- Customer purchase decisions depend in part on availability of third-party software applications and services
- Third-party developers may discontinue development and maintenance of software for Apple's products
- Developer support depends on perceived benefits compared to competitors' platforms (Android, Windows, PlayStation, Nintendo, Xbox)
- Factors affecting developer support: market position, anticipated revenue, expected growth, development costs
## Product and Technology Risks

### Product Development and Innovation
- Ability to compete successfully depends on continuing and timely introduction of innovative new products, services, and technologies
- New products may not achieve market acceptance
- Product life cycles are short
- Dependence on new product introductions and services growth

### Gross Margin Volatility
- Future gross margins can be impacted by a variety of factors
- Gross margins subject to volatility and downward pressure
- Products gross margin affected by: favorable/unfavorable costs, product mix, tariff costs, higher costs (including memory)
- Services gross margin affected by: higher Services net sales, mix of services, higher costs
## Geographic and Market Risks

### Greater China Market
- Greater China revenue declined 4% in FY2025 ($64.4B vs. $66.9B in FY2024)
- Continued volatility in Greater China market could materially affect results

### International Operations and Currency Fluctuations
- International operations expose the Company to foreign exchange risk
- Currency fluctuations can materially affect results of operations and financial condition
- The Company uses derivative instruments to partially offset foreign exchange risk, but may not hedge all exposures
- No assurance that hedges will offset more than a portion of financial impact

### Trade Restrictions and Tariffs
- Restrictions on international trade can increase cost or limit availability of products and components
- Tariff costs have impacted and may continue to impact gross margins
- Potential for additional tariffs, trade restrictions, or other governmental actions

### Legal Proceedings and Claims
- Subject to various legal proceedings and claims in ordinary course of business
- Outcomes are inherently uncertain
- May be subject to fines, penalties, or settlements that could materially affect financial condition
- Management believes there is not at least a reasonable possibility of material loss concerning asserted legal and other claims

### Regulatory Compliance
- Subject to various federal, state, local, and international laws and regulations
- Non-compliance could result in fines, penalties, or restrictions on operations
- Increasing regulatory focus on technology companies, data privacy, and competition

### Unrecognized Tax Benefits
- Gross unrecognized tax benefits: $23.2 billion (September 27, 2025)
- $10.6 billion, if recognized, would impact effective tax rate
- Evaluation involves significant judgment in interpretation and application of GAAP and complex domestic/international tax laws
- No assurance that reserves are reasonable or that final outcomes will not differ
- Could decrease by up to $6 billion in the next 12 months
- Effective tax rate volatility due to changes in unrecognized tax benefits

### State Aid Decision
- $10.7 billion year-over-year decrease in provision for income taxes related to State Aid Decision
- Ongoing tax disputes and examinations

### Tax Legislation
- Subject to potential changes in tax laws and regulations
- U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA) impacts
- Deemed repatriation tax payable: $8.8 billion (within 12 months)

### Cybersecurity Threats
- Management responsibility led by Head of Corporate Information Security
- Dedicated Information Security team with extensive experience
- Processes to log, track, address, and escalate cybersecurity incidents
- Enterprise risk management program includes cybersecurity risks
- Audit Committee oversight of cybersecurity matters
- No assurance that security measures will prevent, detect, or mitigate all threats
- Cybersecurity incidents could materially affect business, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price

### Interest Rate Risk
- Exposed to fluctuations in U.S. interest rates
- Impacts investment portfolio and term debt
- Increases in interest rates negatively affect fair value of investments
- Uses interest rate swaps to manage risk on certain debt

### Market Risk
- Exposed to interest rates and foreign exchange rates
- Uses various strategies to manage risks, but they may still impact consolidated financial statements
- Investment portfolio subject to market risk

### Liquidity and Capital Resources
- Relies on continued access to debt markets
- Commercial paper program and term debt obligations
- Share repurchase program and dividend payments require significant cash
- Cash requirements include: debt ($91.3B principal), leases ($16.8B), manufacturing purchase obligations ($56.2B), other purchase obligations ($14.8B), deemed repatriation tax ($8.8B)

### Key Personnel
- Dependence on senior management and key personnel
- Loss of key personnel could materially affect business

### Intellectual Property
- Relies on ability to protect and enforce intellectual property rights
- May be subject to intellectual property infringement claims
- IP disputes could result in significant costs and restrictions

### Natural Disasters and Pandemics
- Manufacturing and supply chain concentrated in specific geographic regions
- Susceptible to natural disasters, pandemics, and other disruptions
- Could cause delays or increases in costs
## Accounting and Reporting Risks

### Critical Accounting Estimates
- Preparation of financial statements requires management judgments, assumptions, and estimates
- Significant accounting policies and estimates affect carrying values of assets and liabilities
- Uncertain tax positions require significant judgment
- Legal and other contingencies require estimates and judgments

### Internal Controls
- Subject to internal control evaluation and auditing
- Material weaknesses or deficiencies could affect financial reporting

## Forward-Looking Statements
- Form 10-K contains forward-looking statements under Private Securities Litigation Reform Act
- Statements regarding macroeconomic conditions, tariffs, and other measures are forward-looking
- Actual results may differ significantly from forward-looking statements
- Factors that might cause differences include those discussed in Risk Factors

### Term Debt (Notes)
Apple has outstanding senior unsecured fixed-rate notes with varying maturities. As of September 27, 2025, the aggregate principal amount of Notes was $91.3 billion.

- **2013-2023 issuances**: Fixed-rate notes ranging from 0.000% to 6.65% effective interest rates, maturities 2025-2062
- **2025 issuance**: $4.5 billion fixed-rate notes (4.000%-4.750%) due 2028-2035, effective interest rate 4.07%-4.83%

**Maturity Schedule (Principal)**:
- 2026: $12.4 billion
- 2027: $10.1 billion
- 2028: $9.3 billion
- 2029: $5.2 billion
- 2030: $5.0 billion
- Thereafter: $49.3 billion
**Future Interest Payments**: $37.0 billion total, with $2.6 billion payable within 12 months

**Hedging Arrangements**:
- Interest rate swaps: Convert fixed rates to floating rates on a portion of U.S. dollar-denominated notes
- Cross-currency swaps: Convert foreign currency-denominated notes to U.S. dollar-denominated notes
- Effective interest rates include interest, amortization, and hedge adjustments

**Key Legal Documents**:

- Used for general corporate purposes including dividends and share repurchases
- Outstanding as of September 27, 2025: $8.0 billion
- Maturities generally less than 9 months
- Weighted-average interest rate: 4.19% (September 27, 2025)

### Operating Leases
- Equipment and facilities: corporate, data centers, manufacturing, retail space
- Original terms: Not exceeding 10 years
- Multiyear renewal options, some reasonably certain of exercise
- Fixed lease costs: $2.1 billion (2025)
- Variable lease costs: $16.1 billion (2025), $13.8 billion (2024), $13.9 billion (2023)
- Fixed cash payments: $2.1 billion (2025)

### Finance Leases

- 2027: $1.99 billion
- 2028: $1.85 billion
- 2029: $1.59 billion
- 2030: $1.38 billion
- Thereafter: $5.96 billion
- Total undiscounted: $14.73 billion

- Imputed interest: $2.24 billion
- Total lease liabilities: $12.49 billion

- Lease terms: 1-21 years

- $55.4 billion payable within 12 months
- Outsourcing partners for subassembly manufacturing and final assembly/testing
- Individual component suppliers

- $7.0 billion payable within 12 months
- Noncancelable obligations for:

## Shareholder Agreements and Equity Plans

### Share Repurchase Program
- **May 2024 Program**: $110 billion authorized
- Utilized $19.8 billion in Q4 2025
- $89.3 billion repurchased in FY2025 (402 million shares)

### Manufacturing Agreements
- Substantially all hardware products manufactured by outsourcing partners
- Primary manufacturing locations: China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam
- Agreements for supply of many components (may not be extendable/renewable on similar terms)
- Custom components often from single sources

### Component Supply
- Multiple suppliers for most components, but certain components from single/limited sources
- Custom components not commonly used by competitors
- New products often utilize custom single-source components
- Agreements entered into for supply of many components
- Risk: May not be able to extend/renew on similar terms, or at all

### Vendor Non-Trade Receivables
- Non-trade receivables from manufacturing vendors resulting from sale of components
- Two vendors individually represented 10% or more of total vendor non-trade receivables
- As of June 27, 2026: 47% and 22% of total
- As of September 27, 2025: 46% and 23% of total
- Company does not reflect component sales in products net sales; recognizes gain as reduction of products cost of sales when related final products are sold
## Distribution and Carrier Contracts

### Cellular Network Carrier Agreements
- Third-party cellular network carriers accounted for 27% of total trade receivables (June 27, 2026)
- Third-party cellular network carriers accounted for 34% of total trade receivables (September 27, 2025)
- Company requires third-party credit support or collateral from certain customers to limit credit risk

### Distribution Rights
- Noncancelable obligations related to distribution rights included in other purchase obligations

### Licensed Intellectual Property and Content
- Noncancelable obligations for licensed intellectual property and content
- Included in other purchase obligations ($14.8 billion total)

### Advertising Services
- Third-party licensing arrangements
- Company's own advertising platforms

## Key Legal Proceedings (Contingencies)
- The Company is subject to various legal proceedings and claims in the ordinary course of business
- Management believes there is not at least a reasonable possibility the Company may have incurred a material loss concerning loss contingencies for asserted legal and other claims
- Outcome of litigation is inherently uncertain

1. **10-K.txt** - Fiscal year ended September 27, 2025 (in filings/current/)
2. **10-Q.txt** - Quarterly period ended June 27, 2026 (in filings/current/)

### Extraction Scope
Extract structured key disclosures from each filing into **pipeline/extracted/** with the following naming convention:
- `AAPL_10-K_20250927_<section>.md` for 10-K sections
- `AAPL_10-Q_20260627_<section>.md` for 10-Q sections

### 10-K Priority Sections (in order)
1. **Item 1 - Business** (products, services, segments, customers, competition)
2. **Item 1A - Risk Factors** (all material risks, quantify where possible)
3. **Item 1B - Unresolved Staff Comments**
4. **Item 1C - Cybersecurity** (governance, incidents, risk management)
5. **Item 2 - Properties** (owned/leased, locations, capacity)
6. **Item 3 - Legal Proceedings** (material litigation, contingencies)
7. **Item 7 - MD&A** (results of operations, liquidity, capital resources, critical accounting estimates)

8. **Item 7A - Quantitative/Qualitative Market Risk** (interest rate, FX, commodity, equity)
9. **Item 8 - Financial Statements** (balance sheet, income statement, cash flows, notes - extract key figures and policies)
10. **Item 9A - Controls and Procedures** (disclosure controls, internal control over financial reporting)
11. **Item 15 - Exhibits** (list only - extractor_2 handles content)

### 10-Q Priority Sections
1. **Item 1 - Financial Statements** (condensed statements, key changes from 10-K)
2. **Item 2 - MD&A** (quarterly results, liquidity updates, material changes)
3. **Item 3 - Market Risk** (changes from 10-K)
4. **Item 4 - Controls and Procedures** (changes from 10-K)
5. **Item 1A - Risk Factors** (updates/additions since 10-K)
6. **Item 6 - Exhibits** (list only)

### Output Format for Each Section
```markdown
# AAPL - [Filing Type] - [Section Name]
**Source**: [Filing filename], [Item number]
**Fiscal Period**: [Period]
**Extraction Date**: [Date]

## Summary
[2-3 paragraph executive summary]

## Key Disclosures
[Structured extraction of all material facts, figures, commitments, contingencies]

## Quantitative Data
[Tables of key metrics with period comparisons]

## Red Flags / Items for Checker
[Anything unusual, vague, or requiring verification]
```

### Deliverables
Place all extractions in `pipeline/extracted/`. Notify checker when complete via note to `board/to_checker/`.

### Deadline
Complete initial extraction by end of Shift 5.

Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm To the Shareholders and the Board of Directors of Apple Inc. Opinion on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting We have audited Apple Inc.’s internal control over financial reporting as of September 27, 2025, based on criteria established in Internal Control – Integrated Framework issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (2013 framework) (the “COSO criteria”). In our opinion, Apple Inc. (the “Company”) maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control over financial reporting as of September 27, 2025, based on the COSO criteria. We also have audited, in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States) (“PCAOB”), the consolidated balance sheets of the Company as of September 27, 2025 and September 28, 2024, the related consolidated statements of operations, comprehensive income, shareholders’ equity and cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended September 27, 2025, and the related notes and our report dated October 31, 2025 expressed an unqualified opinion thereon. Basis for Opinion The Company’s management is responsible for maintaining effective internal control over financial reporting and for its assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting included in the accompanying Management’s Annual Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting. Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company’s internal control over financial reporting based on our audit. We are a public accounting firm registered with the PCAOB and are required to be independent with respect to the Company in accordance with the U.S. federal securities laws and the applicable rules and regulations of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the PCAOB. We conducted our audit in accordance with the standards of the PCAOB. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether effective internal control over financial reporting was maintained in all material respects. Our audit included obtaining an understanding of internal control over financial reporting, assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of internal control based on the assessed risk, and performing such other procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances. We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion. Definition and Limitations of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting A company’s internal control over financial reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorizations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements. Because of its inherent limitations, internal control over financial reporting may not prevent or detect misstatements. Also, projections of any evaluation of effectiveness to future periods are subject to the risk that controls may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.

Inherent Limitations over Internal Controls The Company’s internal control over financial reporting is designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with GAAP. The Company’s internal control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures that: (i) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the Company’s assets; (ii) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with GAAP, and that the Company’s receipts and expenditures are being made only in accordance with authorizations of the Company’s management and directors; and (iii) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition of the Company’s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements. Further, the design of a control system must reflect the fact that there are resource constraints, and the benefits of controls must be considered relative to their costs. Because of the inherent limitations in all control systems, no evaluation of internal controls can provide absolute assurance that all control issues and instances of fraud, if any, have been detected. Services Advertising The Company’s advertising services include third-party licensing arrangements and the Company’s own advertising platforms. AppleCare The
Company offers a portfolio of fee-based service and support products under the AppleCare ® brand. The offerings provide priority access to Apple technical
support, access to the global Apple authorized service network for repair and replacement services, and in many cases additional coverage for instances of

accidental damage or theft and loss, depending on the country and type of product. Cloud Services The Company’s cloud services store and keep customers’
content up-to-date and available across multiple Apple devices and Windows personal computers. Digital Content The Company operates various platforms,
including the App Store ® , that allow customers to discover and download applications and digital content, such as books, music, video, games and podcasts.
The Company also offers digital content through subscription-based services, including Apple Arcade ® , a game service; Apple Fitness+ ® , a personalized
fitness service; Apple Music ® , which offers users a curated listening experience with on-demand radio stations; Apple News+ ® , a news and magazine service;
and Apple TV ® , which offers exclusive original content and live sports. Payment Services The Company offers payment services, including Apple Card ® , a
co-branded credit card, and Apple Pay ® , a cashless payment service. Segments The Company manages its business primarily on a geographic basis. The Company’s
reportable segments consist of the Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific. Americas includes both North and South America. Europe

includes European countries, as well as India, the Middle East and Africa. Greater China includes China mainland, Hong Kong and Taiwan. Rest of Asia Pacific
includes Australia, New Zealand and those Asian countries not included in the Company’s other reportable segments. Although the reportable segments provide
similar hardware and software products and similar services, each one is managed separately to better align with the location of the Company’s customers and
distribution partners and the unique market dynamics of each geographic region. Markets and Distribution The Company’s customers are primarily in the consumer,
small and mid-sized business, education, enterprise and government markets. The Company sells its products and resells third-party products in most of its
major markets directly to customers through its retail and online stores and its direct sales force. The Company sells its services in the same markets through
its various service platforms. The Company also employs a variety of indirect distribution channels, such as third-party cellular network carriers and other
resellers, for the sale of its products and certain of its services. During 2025, the Company’s net sales through its direct and indirect distribution channels

accounted for 40% and 60%, respectively, of total net sales. Competition The markets for the Company’s products and services are highly competitive and are
characterized by aggressive price competition, downward pressure on gross margins, continual improvement in product performance, and price sensitivity on the
part of consumers and businesses. The markets in which the Company competes are further defined by frequent introduction of new products and services, short
product life cycles, evolving industry standards, and rapid adoption of technological advancements by competitors. Many of the Company’s competitors seek to
compete primarily through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures, and by imitating the Company’s products and infringing on its intellectual property.

effectively protect and enforce the Company’s intellectual property rights. The Company is focused on expanding its market opportunities related to
smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories, and services. The Company’s products and services face substantial competition from

markets, and some of the markets in which the Company competes have from time to time experienced little to no growth or contracted overall. Supply of

obtained from single or limited sources. The Company also competes for various components with other participants in the markets for smartphones, personal
computers, tablets, wearables and accessories. Therefore, many components used by the Company, including those that are available from multiple sources, are at
times subject to industry-wide shortage and significant commodity pricing fluctuations. Restrictions on international trade can increase the cost or limit the
availability of the Company’s products and the components and rare earths and other raw materials that go into them. The Company uses some custom components
that are not commonly used by its competitors, and new products introduced by the Company often utilize custom components available from only one source. When

for the supply of components on similar terms, or at all, and may not be successful in obtaining sufficient quantities from its suppliers or in a timely

# Risk Factors - Apple Inc. (AAPL)

## Overview
The Company's business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price can be materially and adversely affected by a number of factors, whether currently known or unknown. These risk factors are detailed in Part I, Item 1A of the 2025 Form 10-K and Part II, Item 1A of the Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 28, 2026.
## Macroeconomic and Industry Risks

### Global Economic Conditions
- Operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions
- Sales outside the U.S. represent a majority of total net sales
- Global supply chain is large and complex; majority of supplier facilities located outside the U.S.
- Adverse macroeconomic conditions (slow growth, recession, high unemployment, inflation, tighter credit, higher interest rates, currency fluctuations) can materially adversely affect demand for products and services
- Consumer confidence and spending can be materially affected by changes in fiscal/monetary policy, financial market volatility, declines in income or asset values
- Uncertainty about economic conditions can significantly impact suppliers, contract manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, carriers, and developers
- Potential outcomes include: financial instability, inability to obtain credit, insolvency

- Can lead to increased credit/collectibility risk on trade receivables, failure of derivative counterparties, limitations on debt issuance, reduced liquidity, declines in fair values of financial instruments
### Supply Chain and Component Risks

#### Supply Constraints and Increasing Costs
- Experiencing supply constraints and increasing costs for components
- Driven by industry supply-demand imbalances for components, including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND), and memory (DRAM)
- Trends expected to intensify, potentially materially negatively impacting revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations, and financial condition
- Actions like price increases may not effectively mitigate negative impacts and may reduce demand

#### Single/Limited Source Suppliers
- Certain components currently obtained from single or limited sources
- Custom components not commonly used by competitors
- New products often utilize custom components available from only one source
- Initial capacity constraints may exist for new technology components until supplier yields mature or capacities increase
- May not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all
- May not successfully obtain sufficient quantities from suppliers in a timely manner
- Component suppliers may fail, consolidate, or decide to concentrate on common components instead of customized components
- Substantially all hardware products manufactured by outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam

#### Computing Resources and AI/ML
- Business depends on access to sufficient computing resources
- Demand for cloud computing and AI infrastructure has increased substantially across the technology industry
- Constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs
- Relies on third-party cloud service providers to meet compute needs
- May be unable to secure sufficient capacity on commercially reasonable terms, or at all
- If unable to obtain adequate compute capacity timely or at reasonable rates, could limit functionality/availability of products/services, delay new features, or cause significantly higher costs
- May over- or under-estimate requirements, resulting in higher-than-expected costs or inability to satisfy customer demand

### Intense Competition
- Markets are highly competitive with aggressive price competition and downward pressure on gross margins
- Characterized by continual improvement in product performance and price sensitivity
- Frequent introduction of new products and services, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid adoption of technological advancements
- Competitors seek to compete through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures
- Competitors imitate products and infringe on intellectual property
- Apple has minority market share in global smartphone, PC, tablet, and wearables markets
- Some markets have experienced little to no growth or contracted overall

- Competitors have broad product lines, low-priced products, large installed bases, and large customer bases
- Certain competitors have resources/experience/cost structures to provide products/services at little or no profit or even at a loss

### Developer Ecosystem
- Future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers
- Customer purchase decisions depend in part on availability of third-party software applications and services
- Third-party developers may discontinue development and maintenance of software for Apple's products
- Developer support depends on perceived benefits compared to competitors' platforms (Android, Windows, PlayStation, Nintendo, Xbox)
- Factors affecting developer support: market position, anticipated revenue, expected growth, development costs
## Product and Technology Risks

### Product Development and Innovation
- Ability to compete successfully depends on continuing and timely introduction of innovative new products, services, and technologies
- New products may not achieve market acceptance
- Product life cycles are short
- Dependence on new product introductions and services growth

### Gross Margin Volatility
- Future gross margins can be impacted by a variety of factors
- Gross margins subject to volatility and downward pressure
- Products gross margin affected by: favorable/unfavorable costs, product mix, tariff costs, higher costs (including memory)
- Services gross margin affected by: higher Services net sales, mix of services, higher costs
## Geographic and Market Risks

### Greater China Market
- Greater China revenue declined 4% in FY2025 ($64.4B vs. $66.9B in FY2024)
- Continued volatility in Greater China market could materially affect results

### International Operations and Currency Fluctuations
- International operations expose the Company to foreign exchange risk
- Currency fluctuations can materially affect results of operations and financial condition
- The Company uses derivative instruments to partially offset foreign exchange risk, but may not hedge all exposures
- No assurance that hedges will offset more than a portion of financial impact

### Trade Restrictions and Tariffs
- Restrictions on international trade can increase cost or limit availability of products and components
- Tariff costs have impacted and may continue to impact gross margins
- Potential for additional tariffs, trade restrictions, or other governmental actions

### Legal Proceedings and Claims
- Subject to various legal proceedings and claims in ordinary course of business
- Outcomes are inherently uncertain
- May be subject to fines, penalties, or settlements that could materially affect financial condition
- Management believes there is not at least a reasonable possibility of material loss concerning asserted legal and other claims

### Regulatory Compliance
- Subject to various federal, state, local, and international laws and regulations
- Non-compliance could result in fines, penalties, or restrictions on operations
- Increasing regulatory focus on technology companies, data privacy, and competition

### Unrecognized Tax Benefits
- Gross unrecognized tax benefits: $23.2 billion (September 27, 2025)
- $10.6 billion, if recognized, would impact effective tax rate
- Evaluation involves significant judgment in interpretation and application of GAAP and complex domestic/international tax laws
- No assurance that reserves are reasonable or that final outcomes will not differ
- Could decrease by up to $6 billion in the next 12 months
- Effective tax rate volatility due to changes in unrecognized tax benefits

### State Aid Decision
- $10.7 billion year-over-year decrease in provision for income taxes related to State Aid Decision
- Ongoing tax disputes and examinations

### Tax Legislation
- Subject to potential changes in tax laws and regulations
- U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA) impacts
- Deemed repatriation tax payable: $8.8 billion (within 12 months)

### Cybersecurity Threats
- Management responsibility led by Head of Corporate Information Security
- Dedicated Information Security team with extensive experience
- Processes to log, track, address, and escalate cybersecurity incidents
- Enterprise risk management program includes cybersecurity risks
- Audit Committee oversight of cybersecurity matters
- No assurance that security measures will prevent, detect, or mitigate all threats
- Cybersecurity incidents could materially affect business, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price

### Interest Rate Risk
- Exposed to fluctuations in U.S. interest rates
- Impacts investment portfolio and term debt
- Increases in interest rates negatively affect fair value of investments
- Uses interest rate swaps to manage risk on certain debt

### Market Risk
- Exposed to interest rates and foreign exchange rates
- Uses various strategies to manage risks, but they may still impact consolidated financial statements
- Investment portfolio subject to market risk

### Liquidity and Capital Resources
- Relies on continued access to debt markets
- Commercial paper program and term debt obligations
- Share repurchase program and dividend payments require significant cash
- Cash requirements include: debt ($91.3B principal), leases ($16.8B), manufacturing purchase obligations ($56.2B), other purchase obligations ($14.8B), deemed repatriation tax ($8.8B)

### Key Personnel
- Dependence on senior management and key personnel
- Loss of key personnel could materially affect business

### Intellectual Property
- Relies on ability to protect and enforce intellectual property rights
- May be subject to intellectual property infringement claims
- IP disputes could result in significant costs and restrictions

### Natural Disasters and Pandemics
- Manufacturing and supply chain concentrated in specific geographic regions
- Susceptible to natural disasters, pandemics, and other disruptions
- Could cause delays or increases in costs
## Accounting and Reporting Risks

### Critical Accounting Estimates
- Preparation of financial statements requires management judgments, assumptions, and estimates
- Significant accounting policies and estimates affect carrying values of assets and liabilities
- Uncertain tax positions require significant judgment
- Legal and other contingencies require estimates and judgments

- Subject to internal control evaluation and auditing

terms and California law constraints).

indemnification (no advancement for derivative claims, no indemnification for intentional
misconduct or knowing violation of law, no indemnification in a derivative action for
disapproval of a transaction in which the director has a material financial interest). **These
statutory constraints are a matter of California public law, not of the contract text** - they
apply regardless of what the form agreement says, because California law caps what a California
corporation may contractually indemnify. Flagged as the applicable statutory framework, not as a

## A. Accelerated Share Repurchase Agreements (ASRs) - NEW in Q3 FY2026

**Source**: 10-Q.txt Item 2, footnote (2) to the issuer purchases table (line 550)
**Date**: Entered into **May 2026**
**Parties**: Apple Inc. and unnamed financial institutions (banks acting as ASR counterparties)
**Type**: Equity repurchase / derivative-embedded capital return contract

### Key Terms
- **Financial commitments**: financial institutions committed to deliver shares of Apple common
stock during the purchase periods **in exchange for up-front payments totalling $10.0 billion**
- **Settlement mechanics**: total shares ultimately delivered, and therefore the **average
repurchase price paid per share, is determined based on the volume-weighted average price
(VWAP)** of Apple common stock during the ASRs' purchase periods
- **Purchase periods end in the fourth quarter of 2026**
- **Counterparty risk**: the banks are not identified. An ASR is economically a prepaid forward

contract plus an option; the counterparty's credit quality and any early-termination or
price-adjustment (VWAP collar) provisions are not disclosed.

### Due Diligence Flags
- **Change of control**: an ASR outstanding at a transaction date is a genuine deal mechanic -
early termination typically triggers a settlement payment calculated against VWAP up to
termination. If a change of control occurred before Q4 FY2026, up to **$10.0 billion** of
settlement exposure could arise. **The termination/change-of-control clause is not disclosed.**
Flag as a high-priority item.
- **No exhibit filed**: despite being a material derivative-embedded commitment, the ASRs were
**not filed as an exhibit** to the 10-Q. Item 6 of the 10-Q lists only certifications and XBRL.

This is consistent with Apple's practice of treating commercial paper and buyback arrangements
as non-exhibit-reportable, but it does mean **no executed ASR document is available to review**.
- **Counterparty identity unknown** - unmitigated credit and settlement risk.

### Red Flags for Checker
- The $10.0B ASR is the single largest new contractual commitment disclosed in the quarter. It is
**narrative-only**; there is no filed agreement. Any memo statement about ASR terms must be
attributed to the 10-Q narrative, not to an agreement.

transactions, **including under plans complying with Rule 10b5-1** under the Exchange Act.

### Due Diligence Flags
- **Change of control**: because the programmes are expressly **non-obligatory**, a change of
control does not create a repurchase obligation. This is a *favourable* finding and should be

defense:

## 1. Manufacturing and Supply Chain

**Source**: 10-K Note 12 "Concentrations in the Available Sources of Supply of Materials and

assembly and testing of finished products

- **Substantially all** of Apple's hardware products are manufactured by outsourcing partners
located primarily in **China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam**

### Supply concentration - the material contractual risk
- Most components essential to the business are generally available from **multiple sources**
- However, **certain components are obtained from single or limited sources**
- Apple **uses custom components not commonly used by its competitors**, and **new products
introduced by Apple often utilise custom components available from only one source**
- Apple competes for various components with other participants in the smartphone, PC, tablet,
wearable and accessory markets, so even multi-sourced components are subject to industry-wide
shortage and significant commodity pricing fluctuations

- When a component or product uses new technologies, **initial capacity constraints may exist**
until supplier yields mature or capacity increases
- **Express contractual risk statement from the filing**: *"The Company has entered into agreements
for the supply of many components; however, the Company **may not be able to extend or renew
agreements for the supply of components on similar terms, or at all**, and may not be successful
in obtaining sufficient quantities from its suppliers or in a timely manner, or in identifying
and obtaining sufficient quantities from an alternative source."*
- Further: *"component suppliers **may fail, be subject to consolidation** within a particular

industry, or **decide to concentrate on the production of common components** instead of
components customized to meet the Company's requirements"*
- **Restrictions on international trade** can increase cost or limit availability of Apple's
products and of the components and **rare earths and other raw materials** that go into them

- At **9/27/2025**: **46%** and **23%** of the total
- Mechanics: components sold by Apple to manufacturing vendors generate non-trade receivables.
Apple does **not** reflect these component sales in products net sales; it recognises the gain as
a **reduction of products cost of sales when the related final products are sold**.
*This is effectively vendor financing embedded in the supply chain, and it is concentrated in two

## A. Accelerated Share Repurchase Agreements (ASRs) - NEW in Q3 FY2026

**Source**: 10-Q.txt Item 2, footnote (2) to the issuer purchases table (line 550)
**Date**: Entered into **May 2026**
**Parties**: Apple Inc. and unnamed financial institutions (banks acting as ASR counterparties)
**Type**: Equity repurchase / derivative-embedded capital return contract

### Key Terms
- **Financial commitments**: financial institutions committed to deliver shares of Apple common
stock during the purchase periods **in exchange for up-front payments totalling $10.0 billion**
- **Settlement mechanics**: total shares ultimately delivered, and therefore the **average
repurchase price paid per share, is determined based on the volume-weighted average price
(VWAP)** of Apple common stock during the ASRs' purchase periods
- **Purchase periods end in the fourth quarter of 2026**
- **Counterparty risk**: the banks are not identified. An ASR is economically a prepaid forward

contract plus an option; the counterparty's credit quality and any early-termination or
price-adjustment (VWAP collar) provisions are not disclosed.

### Due Diligence Flags
- **Change of control**: an ASR outstanding at a transaction date is a genuine deal mechanic -
early termination typically triggers a settlement payment calculated against VWAP up to
termination. If a change of control occurred before Q4 FY2026, up to **$10.0 billion** of
settlement exposure could arise. **The termination/change-of-control clause is not disclosed.**
Flag as a high-priority item.
- **No exhibit filed**: despite being a material derivative-embedded commitment, the ASRs were
**not filed as an exhibit** to the 10-Q. Item 6 of the 10-Q lists only certifications and XBRL.

This is consistent with Apple's practice of treating commercial paper and buyback arrangements
as non-exhibit-reportable, but it does mean **no executed ASR document is available to review**.
- **Counterparty identity unknown** - unmitigated credit and settlement risk.

### Red Flags for Checker
- The $10.0B ASR is the single largest new contractual commitment disclosed in the quarter. It is

## 1. Manufacturing and Supply Chain

**Source**: 10-K Note 12 "Concentrations in the Available Sources of Supply of Materials and
Product"; MD&A "Manufacturing Purchase Obligations"

- Apple **utilizes several outsourcing partners** to manufacture subassemblies and to perform final
assembly and testing of finished products
- Apple also obtains individual components from a **wide variety of individual suppliers**
- **Substantially all** of Apple's hardware products are manufactured by outsourcing partners
located primarily in **China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam**

### Supply concentration - the material contractual risk
- Most components essential to the business are generally available from **multiple sources**
- However, **certain components are obtained from single or limited sources**
- Apple **uses custom components not commonly used by its competitors**, and **new products
introduced by Apple often utilise custom components available from only one source**
- Apple competes for various components with other participants in the smartphone, PC, tablet,
wearable and accessory markets, so even multi-sourced components are subject to industry-wide
shortage and significant commodity pricing fluctuations

- When a component or product uses new technologies, **initial capacity constraints may exist**
until supplier yields mature or capacity increases
- **Express contractual risk statement from the filing**: *"The Company has entered into agreements
for the supply of many components; however, the Company **may not be able to extend or renew
agreements for the supply of components on similar terms, or at all**, and may not be successful
in obtaining sufficient quantities from its suppliers or in a timely manner, or in identifying
and obtaining sufficient quantities from an alternative source."*
- Further: *"component suppliers **may fail, be subject to consolidation** within a particular

industry, or **decide to concentrate on the production of common components** instead of
components customized to meet the Company's requirements"*
- **Restrictions on international trade** can increase cost or limit availability of Apple's
products and of the components and **rare earths and other raw materials** that go into them

### Vendor non-trade receivables (concentration disclosure)
- Two vendors individually represented **10% or more** of total vendor non-trade receivables
- At **6/27/2026**: **47%** and **22%** of the total
- At **9/27/2025**: **46%** and **23%** of the total
- Mechanics: components sold by Apple to manufacturing vendors generate non-trade receivables.
Apple does **not** reflect these component sales in products net sales; it recognises the gain as
a **reduction of products cost of sales when the related final products are sold**.
*This is effectively vendor financing embedded in the supply chain, and it is concentrated in two

**Long-term supply prepayments (additional to the receivables above)**: the 10-K discloses that
*"the Company has made prepayments associated with long-term supply agreements to secure supply of
inventory components"*, and identifies credit risk on **trade receivables, vendor non-trade
receivables and long-term prepayments** together as a risk factor. **No amount for these
prepayments is disclosed in the 10-K or 10-Q.** The related risk factor notes vendor non-trade
receivables *"were concentrated among a few individual vendors located primarily in Asia"* and that
failure to monitor and limit exposure *"could be materially adversely affected"*.

### Due Diligence Flags
1. **Single-source custom components are the highest-severity supply risk.** The filings
expressly say new products rely on single-source custom components. A change of control can
trigger customer notification, re-qualification or price renegotiation in custom-component
supply agreements - **and none of those agreements is available for review.**
2. **Assignment/change-of-control consent risk is unquantifiable.** With $57.0B of manufacturing
purchase obligations and effectively all hardware outsourced across six Asian jurisdictions, a
change of control plausibly requires consents across a large supplier base. **No consent

requirement is disclosed anywhere.**
3. **Vendor financing concentration**: 47% + 22% = **69% of vendor non-trade receivables with two
vendors** at 6/27/2026, up from 69% at 9/27/2025. These counterparties are unnamed. Ask:
who are they, what are the payment terms, and is there any security or guarantee?
4. **Trade-restriction exposure**: the filing flags international trade restrictions and rare
earths. Tariff or export-control action is a contractual-cost event as much as a regulatory one.

(as amended and restated effective February 24, 2026)
On November 4, 2025, the Board adopted this amended and restated Apple Inc. Non-Employee Director Plan (the “ Plan ”)

subject to and effective upon approval by the Company’s shareholders at the Annual Meeting on February 24, 2026. The Plan was formerly known as the 1997 Director Stock Option Plan and the 1997 Director Stock Plan and was re-named the Non-Employee
Director Plan , subject to approval by the Company’s shareholders at the Annual Meeting on February 13, 2018 . For the terms and conditions of the Plan applicable to an Award, refer to the
version of the Plan in effect as of the date such Award was granted.

1. PURPOSES . The
purposes of the Plan are to retain the services of qualified individuals who are not employees of the Company to serve as members of the Board and to secure for the Company the benefits of the incentives inherent in increased Common Stock ownership
by such individuals by granting such individuals Awards in respect of Shares.

2. ADMINISTRATION .
The Administrator shall be responsible for administering the Plan. Subject to the provisions of the Plan, the Administrator shall have the full authority, in its sole discretion, to take any actions it deems necessary or advisable for the
administration of the Plan, including but not limited to:
(a) determining the Fair Market Value for purposes of any Award;
(b) approving any forms of Award Agreements to be used under the Plan;
(c) amending any outstanding Awards;

(d) construing and interpreting the Plan and any agreements defining the rights and obligations of the Company and Non-Employee
Directors under the Plan;
(e) correcting any defect, supplying any omission or reconciling any inconsistency in the Plan or any Award Agreement;
(f) adopting such rules or guidelines as it deems appropriate to implement the Plan;

(g) authorizing any person to execute on behalf of the Company any instrument required to effect the grant of an Award previously
authorized by the Administrator or the Plan;

(h) adjusting the number of shares subject to any Award, adjusting the price of any or all outstanding Options or otherwise changing
previously imposed terms and conditions, in such circumstances as the Administrator may deem appropriate;
(i) determining whether, and the extent to which, adjustments are required pursuant to Section 7 hereof; and
(j) making all other decisions relating to the operation of the Plan.

Each interpretation, determination, or other action made or taken by the Administrator pursuant to the Plan shall be final and binding on all persons, and the Administrator ’s determinations under the Plan need not be the same for all persons . The Administrator shall not be liable for any action or determination made in good faith, and shall be entitled to
indemnification and reimbursement in the manner provided in the Company ’s Articles of Incorporation and Bylaws as such documents may be amended from time to time.

(a) SHARE LIMIT . Subject to the provisions of Section
7, the maximum number of Shares that may be issued under the Plan shall not exceed 44,800,000 Shares (the “ Share Limit ”). The stock issuable under the Plan shall be authorized and unissued
Shares.

(b) SHARE COUNT . Shares issued pursuant to Restricted
Stock Unit Awards shall count against the Share Limit as two (2) Shares for every one (1) Share issued in connection with the Award. Shares issued pursuant to the exercise of Options shall count against the Share Limit as one (1) Share for every
one (1) Share to which such exercise relates. If Awards are settled in cash, the shares that would have been delivered had there been no cash settlement shall not be counted against the Share Limit. Except as provided in the next sentence, if
Awards are forfeited or are terminated for any reason before settlement or exercise, then the Shares underlying such Awards shall again become available for Awards under the Plan, provided that any one (1) Share subject to a Restricted Stock Unit
Award that is forfeited or terminated shall be credited as two (2) Shares when determining the number of Shares that shall again become available for Awards under the Plan. Shares that are exchanged by a Non-Employee Director or withheld by the
Company as full or partial payment in connection with any Award under the Plan, as well as any Shares exchanged by a Non-Employee Director or withheld by the Company or one of its Subsidiaries to satisfy the tax withholding obligations related to
any Award, shall not be available for subsequent Awards under the Plan.

(c) LIMIT ON COMPENSATION. In no event shall the
compensation payable by the Company to a Non-Employee Director for services performed as a Non-Employee Director, including the grant date value (determined under U.S. generally accepted accounting principles) of Awards, cash retainers, and other
compensation, exceed $1,500,000 in the aggregate in any fiscal year.

Unless otherwise determined by the Administrator, each Non-Employee Director shall receive grants of Restricted Stock Units under the Plan subject to the following provisions of this Section 4 and the terms of any Award Agreement approved by the
Administrator:

(a) ANNUAL GRANTS . On the date of each Annual Meeting
immediately following which a Non-Employee Director is serving on the Board, such Non-Employee Director shall be automatically granted an Award of a number of Restricted Stock Units determined by dividing (i) $310,000 (or such other amount as
determined by the Board prior to the date of such Annual Meeting and subject to the limitations of the Plan) by (ii) the Fair Market Value of the Shares on the date of grant, such number to be rounded to the nearest whole number of Restricted Stock
Units (each, an “ Annual RSU Award ”) .

becomes a Non-Employee Director at any time other than on the date of an Annual Meeting shall be automatically granted, on the date he or she first becomes a Non-Employee Director, an Award of a number of Restricted Stock Units determined by

# AAPL - Form 10-K - Item 3 Legal Proceedings

**Source**: `filings/current/10-K.txt`, Part I, Item 3 (p. 17-18 of the 10-K)
**Fiscal Period**: FY2025 (fiscal year ended September 27, 2025)
**Extraction Date**: Shift 11
**Extracted by**: extractor_1

Apple discloses four categories of legal proceedings: (1) EU Digital Markets Act investigations, (2) a
US Department of Justice civil antitrust lawsuit, (3) the Epic Games litigation, and (4) other
ordinary-course proceedings. The two most financially material are the DMA matters (a €500M fine
already imposed plus a second investigation carrying a fine ceiling of **up to 10% of annual worldwide
net sales**, i.e. up to roughly $41.6B on FY2025 revenue) and the Epic Games injunction, which
directly attacks App Store commission economics.

The 10-Q (`AAPL_10-Q_20260627_legal_proceedings.md`) carries these forward with two material
escalations: the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to allow
Apple to charge a commission, and Apple remains under a US court order preventing it from imposing
any commission or fee on certain purchases.

### 1. EU Digital Markets Act — Article 5(4) Investigation
- **March 25, 2024**: European Commission opened a formal noncompliance investigation under
Article 5(4) of the EU DMA
- Subject matter: how developers may communicate and promote offers to end users for apps
distributed through the App Store, and how developers may conclude contracts with those end users
- **April 23, 2025**: Commission **fined the Company €500 million** and issued a **cease and desist
order** requiring Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions preventing developers from
steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store
- **Apple has appealed** the Article 5(4) decision

### 2. EU DMA — Article 6(4) Investigation
- **June 24, 2024**: Commission opened an additional formal investigation into whether Apple's new
contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces violate the DMA
- **April 23, 2025**: Commission issued **preliminary findings**
- **Financial exposure**: if the Commission makes a final determination of violation it can issue a
cease and desist order and "may impose fines up to 10% of the Company's annual worldwide net sales"
(i.e. up to ~$41.6B based on FY2025 net sales of $416,161M)
- The Commission may seek **additional fines** if it deems Apple violated a cease and desist order

- Apple's position: "The Company believes that it complies with the DMA and has continued to make
changes to its compliance plan in response to feedback and engagement with the Commission."

### 3. Department of Justice Lawsuit
- **March 21, 2024**: DOJ plus a number of state and district attorneys general filed a **civil
antitrust lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey**
- Allegations: monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for **"performance
smartphones"** and **"smartphones"** in violation of US antitrust laws
- **Relief sought: equitable relief** to redress alleged anticompetitive behaviour (note: no monetary
damages sought by DOJ in the disclosed description)
- **Additionally**, various civil litigation matters have been filed in state and federal courts in

the US alleging similar violations and **seeking monetary damages and other nonmonetary relief**
- Apple's position: "The Company believes it has substantial defenses and intends to vigorously defend
itself."

### 4. Epic Games
- **Filed**: US District Court for the Northern District of California ("California District Court"),
by Epic Games, Inc., alleging violations of federal and state antitrust laws and California's unfair
competition law based on Apple's operation of its App Store
- **2021 Injunction**: the California District Court found certain provisions of Apple's App Review
Guidelines violate California's unfair competition law and enjoined Apple from prohibiting developers
from including in their apps buttons, external links or other calls to action directing customers to
purchasing mechanisms other than Apple's in-app purchase system. Applies to apps on the **US

storefronts of the iOS and iPadOS App Stores**
- **January 16, 2024**: Apple implemented a plan to comply and filed a statement of compliance
- **September 30, 2024**: Apple filed a motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction
- **April 30, 2025**: California District Court found Apple **in violation of the 2021 Injunction**
and enjoined Apple from: (a) imposing any commission or any fee on purchases consumers make outside
an app; (b) restricting, conditioning, limiting or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to
purchases outside an app; (c) otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of
an app

- The court **denied** Apple's motion to narrow or vacate, and **referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney
for the Northern District of California to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are
appropriate** — an unusual and material escalation
- Apple appealed to the **Ninth Circuit Court**; the request to stay the decision pending appeal was
**denied**; the Ninth Circuit agreed to hear the appeal on an **expedited basis, with oral arguments
heard in October 2025**
- Apple's position: "The Company will continue to vigorously defend its actions and employees"

### 5. Other Legal Proceedings
- Various proceedings and claims arising in the ordinary course, not fully resolved
- **The Company settled certain matters during Q4 FY2025 that did not individually or in the
aggregate have a material impact on the Company's financial condition or operating results**
- Standard contingency language: outcome of litigation is inherently uncertain; resolution against
the Company for amounts above management's expectations could materially adversely affect results for
that reporting period

| Matter | Amount | Certainty | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| DMA Art. 5(4) fine (imposed 2025-04-23) | €500 million | **Determined** | Item 3 |
| DMA Art. 6(4) maximum fine | up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales (~$41.6B on FY2025 net sales) | Contingent on final determination | Item 3 |
| DMA Art. 6(4) additional fines for CDO breach | Not quantified | Contingent | Item 3 |
| DOJ civil antitrust suit | Equitable relief sought (no quantified damages disclosed) | Contingent | Item 3 |
| Other US state/federal antitrust suits | Monetary damages + nonmonetary relief, unquantified | Contingent | Item 3 |
| Epic Games injunction | Commission/fee prohibition on off-app purchases — revenue impact unquantified | In effect, under appeal | Item 3 |
| Q4 FY2025 settlements | Not material individually or in aggregate (no amount disclosed) | Resolved | Item 3 |
## Red Flags / Items for Checker

1. **The €500M DMA fine is the only quantified adverse legal determination.** No loss contingency
accrual for it is disclosed in the litigation note text. **Checker should confirm from the
Commitments and Contingencies note whether the €500M was expensed/accrued and in which period.**
2. **The DMA Art. 6(4) ceiling of 10% of worldwide net sales** is the single largest quantified
contingent exposure in the filings. It is contingent on a final determination that has not
occurred. Note that preliminary findings are not a final determination.
3. **Criminal contempt referral** in the Epic Games matter is an unusual disclosure and is not
quantified. The 10-Q shows the injunction remains operative, which directly threatens App Store

commission revenue.
4. **The DOJ seeks equitable relief only** as described — but the parallel private suits seek
monetary damages. The distinction matters for exposure modelling and should be preserved.
5. Apple discloses **no accrued loss contingency amounts** in Item 3 itself. The 10-Q Note 9
states management's opinion that "there was not at least a reasonable possibility the Company may
have incurred a material loss, or a material loss greater than a recorded accrual, concerning loss
contingencies for asserted legal and other claims." This appears to be **in tension** with the
€500M fine actually imposed and the 10%-of-sales ceiling. Flag for checker.

6. Apple states it **settled certain matters in Q4 FY2025** but gives no amount — only that they were
not material. The identity of those matters is not disclosed.

# AAPL - Form 10-K - Items 1B, 1C, 2 (Staff Comments, Cybersecurity, Properties)

**Source**: `filings/current/10-K.txt`, Part I, Items 1B, 1C and 2 (pp. 16-17 of the 10-K)
