# Risk Factors - Apple Inc. (AAPL)

## Overview
The Company's business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price can be materially and adversely affected by a number of factors, whether currently known or unknown. These risk factors are detailed in Part I, Item 1A of the 2025 Form 10-K and Part II, Item 1A of the Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 28, 2026.
## Macroeconomic and Industry Risks

### Global Economic Conditions
- Operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions
- Sales outside the U.S. represent a majority of total net sales
- Global supply chain is large and complex; majority of supplier facilities located outside the U.S.
- Adverse macroeconomic conditions (slow growth, recession, high unemployment, inflation, tighter credit, higher interest rates, currency fluctuations) can materially adversely affect demand for products and services
- Consumer confidence and spending can be materially affected by changes in fiscal/monetary policy, financial market volatility, declines in income or asset values
- Uncertainty about economic conditions can significantly impact suppliers, contract manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, carriers, and developers
- Potential outcomes include: financial instability, inability to obtain credit, insolvency

- Can lead to increased credit/collectibility risk on trade receivables, failure of derivative counterparties, limitations on debt issuance, reduced liquidity, declines in fair values of financial instruments
### Supply Chain and Component Risks

#### Supply Constraints and Increasing Costs
- Experiencing supply constraints and increasing costs for components
- Driven by industry supply-demand imbalances for components, including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND), and memory (DRAM)
- Trends expected to intensify, potentially materially negatively impacting revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations, and financial condition
- Actions like price increases may not effectively mitigate negative impacts and may reduce demand

#### Single/Limited Source Suppliers
- Certain components currently obtained from single or limited sources
- Custom components not commonly used by competitors
- New products often utilize custom components available from only one source
- Initial capacity constraints may exist for new technology components until supplier yields mature or capacities increase
- May not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all
- May not successfully obtain sufficient quantities from suppliers in a timely manner
- Component suppliers may fail, consolidate, or decide to concentrate on common components instead of customized components
- Substantially all hardware products manufactured by outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam

#### Computing Resources and AI/ML
- Business depends on access to sufficient computing resources
- Demand for cloud computing and AI infrastructure has increased substantially across the technology industry
- Constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs
- Relies on third-party cloud service providers to meet compute needs
- May be unable to secure sufficient capacity on commercially reasonable terms, or at all
- If unable to obtain adequate compute capacity timely or at reasonable rates, could limit functionality/availability of products/services, delay new features, or cause significantly higher costs
- May over- or under-estimate requirements, resulting in higher-than-expected costs or inability to satisfy customer demand

### Intense Competition
- Markets are highly competitive with aggressive price competition and downward pressure on gross margins
- Characterized by continual improvement in product performance and price sensitivity
- Frequent introduction of new products and services, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid adoption of technological advancements
- Competitors seek to compete through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures
- Competitors imitate products and infringe on intellectual property
- Apple has minority market share in global smartphone, PC, tablet, and wearables markets
- Some markets have experienced little to no growth or contracted overall

- Competitors have broad product lines, low-priced products, large installed bases, and large customer bases
- Certain competitors have resources/experience/cost structures to provide products/services at little or no profit or even at a loss

### Developer Ecosystem
- Future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers
- Customer purchase decisions depend in part on availability of third-party software applications and services
- Third-party developers may discontinue development and maintenance of software for Apple's products
- Developer support depends on perceived benefits compared to competitors' platforms (Android, Windows, PlayStation, Nintendo, Xbox)
- Factors affecting developer support: market position, anticipated revenue, expected growth, development costs
## Product and Technology Risks

### Product Development and Innovation
- Ability to compete successfully depends on continuing and timely introduction of innovative new products, services, and technologies
- New products may not achieve market acceptance
- Product life cycles are short
- Dependence on new product introductions and services growth

### Gross Margin Volatility
- Future gross margins can be impacted by a variety of factors
- Gross margins subject to volatility and downward pressure
- Products gross margin affected by: favorable/unfavorable costs, product mix, tariff costs, higher costs (including memory)
- Services gross margin affected by: higher Services net sales, mix of services, higher costs
## Geographic and Market Risks

### Greater China Market
- Greater China revenue declined 4% in FY2025 ($64.4B vs. $66.9B in FY2024)
- Continued volatility in Greater China market could materially affect results

### International Operations and Currency Fluctuations
- International operations expose the Company to foreign exchange risk
- Currency fluctuations can materially affect results of operations and financial condition
- The Company uses derivative instruments to partially offset foreign exchange risk, but may not hedge all exposures
- No assurance that hedges will offset more than a portion of financial impact

### Trade Restrictions and Tariffs
- Restrictions on international trade can increase cost or limit availability of products and components
- Tariff costs have impacted and may continue to impact gross margins
- Potential for additional tariffs, trade restrictions, or other governmental actions

### Legal Proceedings and Claims
- Subject to various legal proceedings and claims in ordinary course of business
- Outcomes are inherently uncertain
- May be subject to fines, penalties, or settlements that could materially affect financial condition
- Management believes there is not at least a reasonable possibility of material loss concerning asserted legal and other claims

### Regulatory Compliance
- Subject to various federal, state, local, and international laws and regulations
- Non-compliance could result in fines, penalties, or restrictions on operations
- Increasing regulatory focus on technology companies, data privacy, and competition

### Unrecognized Tax Benefits
- Gross unrecognized tax benefits: $23.2 billion (September 27, 2025)
- $10.6 billion, if recognized, would impact effective tax rate
- Evaluation involves significant judgment in interpretation and application of GAAP and complex domestic/international tax laws

### Tax Legislation
- Subject to potential changes in tax laws and regulations

- Deemed repatriation tax payable: $8.8 billion (within 12 months)

### Cybersecurity Threats
- Management responsibility led by Head of Corporate Information Security
- Dedicated Information Security team with extensive experience
- Processes to log, track, address, and escalate cybersecurity incidents

- No assurance that security measures will prevent, detect, or mitigate all threats
- Cybersecurity incidents could materially affect business, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price

### Interest Rate Risk
- Exposed to fluctuations in U.S. interest rates
- Impacts investment portfolio and term debt
- Increases in interest rates negatively affect fair value of investments
- Uses interest rate swaps to manage risk on certain debt

### Market Risk
- Exposed to interest rates and foreign exchange rates
- Uses various strategies to manage risks, but they may still impact consolidated financial statements
- Investment portfolio subject to market risk

### Liquidity and Capital Resources
- Relies on continued access to debt markets
- Commercial paper program and term debt obligations
- Share repurchase program and dividend payments require significant cash
- Cash requirements include: debt ($91.3B principal), leases ($16.8B), manufacturing purchase obligations ($56.2B), other purchase obligations ($14.8B), deemed repatriation tax ($8.8B)

### Key Personnel
- Dependence on senior management and key personnel
- Loss of key personnel could materially affect business

### Intellectual Property
- Relies on ability to protect and enforce intellectual property rights
- May be subject to intellectual property infringement claims
- IP disputes could result in significant costs and restrictions

### Natural Disasters and Pandemics
- Manufacturing and supply chain concentrated in specific geographic regions
- Susceptible to natural disasters, pandemics, and other disruptions
- Could cause delays or increases in costs

- Significant accounting policies and estimates affect carrying values of assets and liabilities

- Legal and other contingencies require estimates and judgments

On April 30, 2025, the California District Court found the Company to be in violation of the 2021 Injunction and enjoined the Company from imposing any commission or any fee on purchases that consumers make outside an app; restricting, conditioning, limiting, or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to purchases outside an app; or otherwise interfering with a consumer’s choice to proceed in or out of an app (the “2025 Injunction”). The Company appealed the California District Court’s April 2025 decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (“Ninth Circuit Court”). On December 11, 2025, the Ninth Circuit Court issued an order upholding the 2025 Injunction in part and modifying certain aspects to allow the Company to require parity in size, form and placement between the Company’s in-app purchase and any links for consumers to make purchases outside an app. The Ninth Circuit Court also held that the Company can charge some commission on link-out purchases, and remanded to the California District Court to further amend or modify the 2025 Injunction, consistent with the Ninth Circuit Court’s order. On May 21, 2026, the Company filed a petition seeking Supreme Court review of the Ninth Circuit Court’s opinion. On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court granted the Company’s petition to review the applicable legal standard for civil contempt. The Company is seeking a stay of the California District Court proceedings pending the Supreme Court’s decision on the question under review. Risk Factors The Company’s business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition and stock price can be materially and adversely affected by a number of factors, whether currently known or unknown, including those described in Part I, Item 1A of the 2025 Form 10-K and Part II, Item 1A of the Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 28, 2026 (the “second quarter 2026 Form 10-Q”), in each case under the heading “Risk Factors.” Except for the risk factors set forth below and those disclosed in Part II, Item 1A of the second quarter 2026 Form 10-Q , which are incorporated by reference herein, there have been no material changes to the Company’s risk factors since the 2025 Form 10-K. Future operating results depend upon the Company’s ability to obtain components and computing resources in sufficient quantities and on commercially reasonable terms. The Company currently obtains certain components from single or limited sources, which exposes it to significant supply and pricing risks. In addition, many components, including those that are available from multiple sources, are at times subject to industry-wide shortages and significant commodity pricing fluctuations that can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price. For example, the Company is experiencing a period of supply constraints and increasing costs for components driven by factors such as industry supply-demand imbalances for components, including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND) and memory (DRAM), which adversely affects the Company’s ability to obtain sufficient quantities of components and products on commercially reasonable terms, or at all. The Company expects these trends to intensify, which may materially adversely impact the Company’s revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations and financial condition. Actions, such as price increases, that have been and may in the future be taken by the Company may not effectively mitigate these negative impacts, and may also reduce demand for the Company’s products and materially adversely affect the Company’s revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations and financial condition. Additionally, the Company’s new products often utilize custom components available from only one source. When a component or product uses new technologies, initial capacity constraints may exist until the suppliers’ yields have matured or their manufacturing capacities have increased. The Company may not be able to extend or renew agreements for the supply of components on similar terms, or at all, and may not be successful in obtaining sufficient quantities from its suppliers in a timely manner, or in identifying and obtaining sufficient quantities from an alternative source. In addition, component suppliers may fail, be subject to consolidation within a particular industry, or decide to concentrate on the production of common components instead of components customized to meet the Company’s requirements, further limiting the Company’s ability to obtain sufficient quantities of components on commercially reasonable terms, or at all. The Company’s business, including its artificial intelligence and machine learning offerings, also depends on access to sufficient computing resources. Demand for cloud computing and artificial intelligence infrastructure has increased substantially across the technology industry, resulting in constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs. In addition to its own data center infrastructure, the Company relies on third-party cloud service providers to meet these compute needs, and the Company may be unable to secure sufficient capacity on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, to meet customer demand. If the Company is unable to obtain adequate compute capacity in a timely manner or at commercially reasonable rates, this can limit the functionality and availability of its products and services, delay the deployment of new features or offerings, or cause the Company to incur significantly higher costs to operate its business, any of which could materially adversely affect the Company’s revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations, and financial condition. In addition, the Company may over- or under-estimate requirements, either of which could result in higher-than-expected costs for the Company or an inability to fully satisfy customer demand. Therefore, the Company remains subject to significant risks of supply shortages and price increases that can materially adversely affect its business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price. The Company’s future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers. The Company believes decisions by customers to purchase its hardware products depend in part on the availability of third-party software applications and services. Third-party developers may discontinue the development and maintenance of software applications and services for the Company’s products. If third-party software applications and services cease to be developed and maintained for the Company’s products, customers may choose not to buy the Company’s products, materially adversely impacting the Company’s business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price. ## The problem, stated plainly

`filings/current/` contains only `10-K.txt`, `10-Q.txt` and `8-K.txt`. **There is no EX-10 text in
the workspace.** Every EX-10.x and most EX-4.x items on Apple's exhibit index are incorporated by
reference from prior S-8 / S-3 / 8-K filings. My assignment from shift 4 anticipated this ("no EX-10
filings visible yet... may arrive later") - they have not arrived, and for Apple they will not,
because Apple does not file individual commercial contracts as exhibits.
So the honest position on my three headline topics:

- **Covenants**: not disclosed. The 10-K's own footnote (1) says instruments defining holders'
rights of long-term debt securities are **omitted under Item 601(b)(4)(iii) of Reg S-K** with an
undertaking to furnish to the SEC on request. That is the covenant package, and it is withheld.
- **Indemnities**: EX-10.2 is a form indemnification agreement with each director and executive
officer **dated 2009-06-27 - 16 years stale** and not re-filed. Scope, whether it is primary or
excess to D&O insurance, and change-in-control triggers are all unavailable. California
Corporations Code 317-318 caps what the agreement can cover, but the contract text is missing.
- **Termination clauses**: not disclosed anywhere, for any contract.

- **Change of control**: two favourable findings and six gaps - see the table in my note to
`summariser`, or `pipeline/extracted/AAPL_indemnification_change_of_control.md`.
- **Governing law**: indeterminate for every contract. BNY Mellon Trust Company N.A. as trustee
*suggests* New York for the indentures; Apple's incorporation is California. Both are inferences,
and I have labelled them as such rather than writing them into the memo as facts.

**Please request these from EDGAR.** They are the documents that would turn the covenant, indemnity
and change-of-control sections of the memo from "identified gap" into analysis:

|---|---|---|
| 4.2 / 4.19 / 4.26 | Indentures 2013-04-29, 2018-11-05, 2021-10-28 | Only source for covenants, change-of-control put, events of default, governing law on $82.3B of notes |

| 97.1 | Rule 10D-1 Recovery Policy (clawback) | Interacts with any change of control |

- **Target**: Apple Inc. (AAPL, CIK 0000320193), California corporation

### Headline finding: NO EX-10 documents are in the workspace
`filings/current/` contains only the three filings. **Every EX-10.x and most EX-4.x items on
Apple's exhibit index are marked with an asterisk and incorporated by reference from a prior
S-8 / S-3 / 8-K filing.** The operative contract text is not available.

The 10-K itself adds footnote (1) to the exhibit index: certain instruments defining holders' rights
of long-term debt securities are **omitted under Item 601(b)(4)(iii) of Regulation S-K**, with an
undertaking to furnish to the SEC on request. That is where the debt covenants would be.

**Implication for the whole review: the covenant package, change-of-control mechanics and
governing law for ~$82.3B of Apple notes, plus the D&O indemnification terms, are simply not in
the file.** Everything must be written up as "described in the exhibit index" not "the contract
provides".

distribution arrangements; supply concentration; **vendor non-trade receivables 47%+22% at

(9.8yr WA term, 3.4% discount rate, $523M uncommenced with **1 to 21 year** terms, variable

# Risk Factors - Apple Inc. (AAPL)

## Overview
The Company's business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price can be materially and adversely affected by a number of factors, whether currently known or unknown. These risk factors are detailed in Part I, Item 1A of the 2025 Form 10-K and Part II, Item 1A of the Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 28, 2026.
## Macroeconomic and Industry Risks

### Global Economic Conditions
- Operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions
- Sales outside the U.S. represent a majority of total net sales
- Global supply chain is large and complex; majority of supplier facilities located outside the U.S.
- Adverse macroeconomic conditions (slow growth, recession, high unemployment, inflation, tighter credit, higher interest rates, currency fluctuations) can materially adversely affect demand for products and services
- Consumer confidence and spending can be materially affected by changes in fiscal/monetary policy, financial market volatility, declines in income or asset values
- Uncertainty about economic conditions can significantly impact suppliers, contract manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, carriers, and developers
- Potential outcomes include: financial instability, inability to obtain credit, insolvency

- Can lead to increased credit/collectibility risk on trade receivables, failure of derivative counterparties, limitations on debt issuance, reduced liquidity, declines in fair values of financial instruments
### Supply Chain and Component Risks

#### Supply Constraints and Increasing Costs
- Experiencing supply constraints and increasing costs for components
- Driven by industry supply-demand imbalances for components, including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND), and memory (DRAM)
- Trends expected to intensify, potentially materially negatively impacting revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations, and financial condition
- Actions like price increases may not effectively mitigate negative impacts and may reduce demand

#### Single/Limited Source Suppliers
- Certain components currently obtained from single or limited sources
- Custom components not commonly used by competitors
- New products often utilize custom components available from only one source
- Initial capacity constraints may exist for new technology components until supplier yields mature or capacities increase
- May not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all
- May not successfully obtain sufficient quantities from suppliers in a timely manner
- Component suppliers may fail, consolidate, or decide to concentrate on common components instead of customized components
- Substantially all hardware products manufactured by outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam

#### Computing Resources and AI/ML
- Business depends on access to sufficient computing resources
- Demand for cloud computing and AI infrastructure has increased substantially across the technology industry
- Constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs
- Relies on third-party cloud service providers to meet compute needs
- May be unable to secure sufficient capacity on commercially reasonable terms, or at all
- If unable to obtain adequate compute capacity timely or at reasonable rates, could limit functionality/availability of products/services, delay new features, or cause significantly higher costs
- May over- or under-estimate requirements, resulting in higher-than-expected costs or inability to satisfy customer demand

### Intense Competition
- Markets are highly competitive with aggressive price competition and downward pressure on gross margins
- Characterized by continual improvement in product performance and price sensitivity
- Frequent introduction of new products and services, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid adoption of technological advancements
- Competitors seek to compete through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures
- Competitors imitate products and infringe on intellectual property
- Apple has minority market share in global smartphone, PC, tablet, and wearables markets
- Some markets have experienced little to no growth or contracted overall

- Competitors have broad product lines, low-priced products, large installed bases, and large customer bases
- Certain competitors have resources/experience/cost structures to provide products/services at little or no profit or even at a loss

### Developer Ecosystem
- Future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers
- Customer purchase decisions depend in part on availability of third-party software applications and services
- Third-party developers may discontinue development and maintenance of software for Apple's products
- Developer support depends on perceived benefits compared to competitors' platforms (Android, Windows, PlayStation, Nintendo, Xbox)
- Factors affecting developer support: market position, anticipated revenue, expected growth, development costs
## Product and Technology Risks

### Product Development and Innovation
- Ability to compete successfully depends on continuing and timely introduction of innovative new products, services, and technologies
- New products may not achieve market acceptance
- Product life cycles are short
- Dependence on new product introductions and services growth

### Gross Margin Volatility
- Future gross margins can be impacted by a variety of factors
- Gross margins subject to volatility and downward pressure
- Products gross margin affected by: favorable/unfavorable costs, product mix, tariff costs, higher costs (including memory)
- Services gross margin affected by: higher Services net sales, mix of services, higher costs
## Geographic and Market Risks

### Greater China Market
- Greater China revenue declined 4% in FY2025 ($64.4B vs. $66.9B in FY2024)
- Continued volatility in Greater China market could materially affect results

### International Operations and Currency Fluctuations

**Prepared by:** Partner (Lead Due Diligence Review)
**Target Company:** Apple Inc. (AAPL)
**Date:** 2026-09-28 (Shift 22)

This memorandum presents the comprehensive due diligence review of Apple Inc. (CIK: 0000320193) for the current fiscal period (Q3 FY2026, completed June 27, 2026). The review covers the primary SEC filings including the 10-K (FY2025), 10-Q (Q3 FY2026), and 8-K (Q3 FY2026 results). Extraction of relevant disclosures has been completed by extractor_1 (business/financial) and extractor_2 (contracts/exhibits). An audit has been performed by the checker, identifying several critical gaps requiring attention.

The overall assessment indicates strong financial health with robust cash reserves, significant shareholder returns through buybacks and dividends, and healthy profitability. However, notable gaps remain in the covenant package, change-of-control provisions, and some contract documentation, which must be addressed before final sign-off.

Apple Inc. is a leading technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California. It designs, manufactures, and markets smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables, and services. Key products include the iPhone, Mac, iPad, Apple Watch, and Apple TV. Services represent approximately 26% of total revenue, with the highest growth segment.

Apple's FY2025 income statement shows net sales of **$416,161M (+6.4% YoY)**, gross margin of
**$195,201M (46.9% of sales)**, operating income of **$133,050M (32.0% margin)** and net income of
**$112,010M (26.9% margin)**. The mix shift toward Services continues: Services grew 13.5% to
$109,158M (26.2% of sales) versus Products at $307,003M (+4.1%). Services gross margin is roughly
double the Products gross margin, so the mix shift is the single largest driver of consolidated
margin expansion.

Cash generation is enormous and stable: operating cash flow of **$111,482M** (down 5.7% YoY from
$118,254M despite higher net income, because of a $11,076M drag from changes in other liabilities
versus a $15,552M benefit in FY2024). Capital return is the dominant use of cash: **$90,711M** of buybacks
plus **$15,421M** of dividends in FY2025, against $111,482M of operating cash flow — i.e. capital
return exceeded operating cash flow, funded partly by the maturity/sale of the securities portfolio
($15,195M net investing inflow).

The balance sheet carries **$132,420M** of cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities
($35,934M cash + $18,763M current + $77,723M non-current securities) against **$98,657M** of total
debt (commercial paper $7,979M + current term debt $12,350M + non-current term debt $78,328M) — a

## Red Flags / Items for Checker

1. **Capital return exceeded free cash flow in FY2025** — $106,132M returned vs ~$98,767M of FCF
(107%), and 95% of operating cash flow of $111,482M. The gap was plugged by **$15,195M of net
investing inflow from maturities/sales of marketable securities**. Buybacks are therefore partly
funded by portfolio drawdown, not solely by operations. This is a structural capital-return
dependency to flag.
2. **$8.8B TCJA deemed repatriation tax payable was outstanding and due within 12 months** at
year-end. Subsequently paid in full in FY2026 (see 10-Q extraction) — the risk was real but has
since resolved. Checker should confirm the payment and the P&L/interest charge treatment.

3. **The Notes trade at an 11.4% discount to carrying value** ($80.4B FV vs $90.7B carrying) — legacy
low-coupon debt. No repricing risk while held (all fixed-rate), but refinancing at current rates
would materially increase interest expense. This is the mirror image of the $146.5B securities
portfolio earning market yields.
4. **No revolving or committed credit facility disclosed** for a company with $57.9B of purchase
obligations. Unusual; verify externally.
5. **Manufacturing purchase obligations of $56.2B are 95% due within 12 months** — the company is
contractually committed to fund suppliers within a year, including in the six Asian manufacturing

countries it named as tariff subjects.
6. **$10.0B of future interest on the Notes** is disclosed but no interest-rate sensitivity on this
amount appears in Item 7A (which instead addresses hypothetical rate changes on cash/securities and
fixed-rate debt fair value). There is therefore **no quantified rate sensitivity on the $10.0B
forward interest commitment** — a disclosure gap the checker may want to note.
7. **Apple is a net repayer of term debt** in FY2025 (issued $4,481M net, repaid $10,932M; net
−$6,451M) and reduced commercial paper by $2.0B. Total debt fell $8.0B YoY. The direction of
travel is deleveraging, but the company simultaneously raised the dividend and authorised $100B of
buybacks — so the capital-return capacity is being funded from the balance sheet and portfolio.

# AAPL - Form 10-Q - Debt, Credit Facilities and Capital Return

**Source**: `filings/current/10-Q.txt`, Note 6 "Debt" (p. 10), Part II Item 2 MD&A "Liquidity and
Capital Resources" / "Capital Return Program" (pp. 17-19)
**Period**: Q3 FY2026 — three and nine months ended **June 27, 2026**
**Extraction Date**: Shift 14
**Extracted by**: extractor_1

Apple carries **$85.3B of total debt** at 2026-06-27, down from **$98.7B** at FY2025 year-end, and is
in a **substantial net cash position of ~$61.2B** ($146.5B cash and securities less $85.3B debt).
Debt is now **entirely fixed-rate**; there are **no floating-rate term debt facilities** and **no
revolving credit facility is disclosed** in either the 10-K or the 10-Q.

The single most important development for the memo: **the $8.8B TCJA deemed repatriation tax payable
was fully paid during the first nine months of FY2026** — removing the largest near-term contractual
cash claim identified in the 10-K.

Term debt fair value is now well below carrying value: **$71.2B fair value vs $82.3B carrying
amount** at 2026-06-27 (a $11.1B / 13.5% discount), versus $80.4B vs $90.7B at FY2025 year-end — the
discount widened by roughly $2.6B, signalling a rise in market yields against Apple's fixed coupons.

| Commercial paper (unsecured short-term promissory notes) | 1,997 | 7,979 |
| Term debt — current | 11,007 | 12,350 |
| Term debt — non-current | 71,340 | 78,328 |
| **Total debt (carrying)** | **84,344** | **98,657** |

- Used to fund **dividends and buybacks** (per Note 6), so the CP balance is a lever on capital return

## Red Flags / Items for Checker

1. **Other purchase obligations doubled from $14.8B to $29.3B (+$14.5B) in nine months.** This is the
single largest change in the contractual obligation profile and is unexplained in the 10-Q. It
accompanies (a) gross intangibles rising from $24,950M to $38,220M (+$13,3B) and (b)
non-current other liabilities rising from $41,549M to $55,080M (+$13,5B). The three moves are of
similar magnitude and the 10-Q contains **no business-combination note and no acquisition
disclosure**. This pattern is the strongest single anomaly in the filings and should be escalated.
2. **The $100B buyback authorization appears exhausted.** $89.3B (FY2025) + $61.8B (9M FY2026) =
$151.1B. The next authorization and its size is a live capital-return question for the memo.

3. **Notes trade at a 13.5% discount to carrying value and the discount widened** ($10.3B → $11.1B),
implying legacy low-coupon debt and higher market rates. Existing coupons are fixed and will not
reprice, but refinancing at current rates would raise interest expense.
4. **No revolving or committed credit facility is disclosed** for a company with $146.5B of liquid
assets and $57.0B of manufacturing purchase obligations. The absence is unusual. Verify externally
before concluding none exists.
5. **Commercial paper is being reduced sharply** ($8.0B → $2.0B; $5.9B net repayment) — the company is
deleveraging the short end while repurchasing $62.1B of stock, funded by operating cash flow and

the securities portfolio. Net cash rose from $33.8B to ~$62.2B. Note CP proceeds are explicitly
permitted for "dividends and share repurchases", so this is an opportunistic funding structure.
6. **No new term debt was issued in 9M FY2026** ($0 vs $4,481M prior year). Combined with the
$8.1B repayment, Apple is shrinking its debt stack — a deleveraging posture that reduces financial
risk but also reduces the interest income that supports "other income/(expense), net."
7. **Manufacturing purchase obligations of $57.0B are 98.6% due within 12 months** — near-term
supplier funding commitment against which the company must deliver, while simultaneously
describing "supply constraints and increasing costs for components ... including advanced
semiconductors, storage (NAND) and memory (DRAM)" in the new Q3 risk factor.

# AAPL - Form 10-K - Item 1A Risk Factors

**Source**: `filings/current/10-K.txt`, Part I, Item 1A (pp. 5-15 of the 10-K)
**Fiscal Period**: FY2025 (fiscal year ended September 27, 2025)
**Extraction Date**: Shift 11
**Extracted by**: extractor_1

Apple's risk factors run ~77,000 characters across three risk categories in the order presented:
**Macroeconomic and Industry Risks**, **Business Risks**, and **Legal and Regulatory Compliance
Risks**. Item 1A is the second-longest part of the 10-K after the financial statements, which is
itself a signal of the regulatory environment.
The three most diligence-relevant clusters for this review are:

1. **Tariffs and trade restrictions** — the single largest *named* macro risk, referencing tariffs
imposed on imports from **China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU**, plus an
active **Section 232 semiconductor investigation** by the US Department of Commerce. The company
states it "cannot predict the ultimate impact."
2. **Legal/regulatory** — 9 mentions of antitrust, 13 of regulatory, 8 of privacy, and an express
risk that legal/regulatory outcomes could require Apple to **share innovations with competitors** or
restrict its IP-derived value.
3. **Supply chain concentration** — reliance on single/limited sources and on outsourcing partners
primarily in Asia for final assembly of substantially all hardware.

Notably, **Item 1A contains no standalone data-breach or cybersecurity-incident risk heading**, no
credit-rating risk, and no reference to the EU State Aid Decision (that appears in the 10-Q tax
discussion instead).

### Category ordering in Item 1A
The three category headers appear in the filing in this sequence:
1. **Macroeconomic and Industry Risks** (first)
2. **Business Risks**
3. **Legal and Regulatory Compliance Risks** (last)
### 1. Macroeconomic and Industry Risks

**Tariffs and international trade restrictions (the dominant named risk)**
- "Restrictions on international trade, such as tariffs and other controls on imports or exports of
goods, technology or data, can materially adversely affect the Company's business and supply chain."
- "**Beginning in the second quarter of 2025, new tariffs were announced on imports to the U.S.**"
("U.S. Tariffs"), including additional tariffs on imports from **China, India, Japan, South Korea,
Taiwan, Vietnam and the European Union ("EU")**, among others
- "In response, several countries have imposed, or threatened to impose, **reciprocal tariffs** on
imports from the U.S. and other retaliatory measures"

- "Various modifications to the U.S. Tariffs have been announced and further changes could be made in
the future, which may include additional **sector-based tariffs** or other measures"
- **Section 232 investigation**: "the U.S. Department of Commerce has initiated an investigation under
**Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962**, as amended, into, among other things, imports
of **semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and their derivative products, including
downstream products that contain semiconductors**"
- "The ultimate impact remains uncertain and will depend on several factors, including whether
additional or incremental U.S. Tariffs or other measures are announced or imposed, to what extent

other countries implement tariffs or other retaliatory measures in response, and the overall
magnitude and duration of these measures."
- Escalation risk: "If disputes and conflicts further escalate, actions by governments in response
could be significantly more severe and restrictive."

**Net sales / gross margin volatility and downward pressure**
The company lists the full set of drivers of margin compression, verbatim in substance:
- continued industry-wide global product pricing pressures and product pricing actions in response
- increased competition
- ability to effectively stimulate demand
- compressed product life cycles
- **supply shortages**
- potential increases in the cost of components, outside manufacturing services, and developing,

acquiring and delivering content for services
- ability to manage product quality and warranty costs
- shifts in the mix of products and services, **or in the geographic, currency or channel mix**,
including to the extent regulatory changes require modification of offerings
- **fluctuations in foreign exchange rates**
- inflation and other macroeconomic pressures
- imposition of new or increased tariffs and other trade restrictions, magnitude/duration, and
retaliatory actions

- introduction of new products or services, including **lower-margin** ones
- Conclusion: "gross margins will be subject to volatility and downward pressure"

**Physical and operational disruption**
- Operations, retail stores and facilities in locations **prone to earthquakes and other natural
disasters**; **global climate change** increasing frequency/intensity of natural disasters and
extreme weather
- Interruption risk from fire, power shortages, nuclear power plant accidents, industrial accidents,
terrorist attacks, **ransomware and other cybersecurity attacks**, labour disputes, public health
issues
- Consequences: difficulty or impossibility of manufacturing and delivering products, delays and

inefficiencies in the supply/manufacturing chain, slowdowns and outages in service offerings,
increased costs, reduced consumer spending and demand in affected areas
- Also exposed to **industrial accidents at suppliers and contract manufacturers**

**Competition and innovation**
- Highly competitive global markets: aggressive price competition, downward pressure on gross margins,
continual improvement in product performance, price sensitivity
- Short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid technological adoption
- Significant R&D investment required; "These investments may not achieve expected returns"
- **"The Company has a minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and
wearables markets"**, and some markets "have from time to time experienced little to no growth or
contracted overall"

- **"Competition has been particularly intense as competitors have aggressively cut prices and lowered
product margins."** Certain competitors can sell "at little or no profit or even at a loss"
- Some competitors have broad product lines, low prices, large installed bases of active devices
- Company "expects competition to intensify as competitors imitate the Company's approach to providing
components seamlessly within their offerings"
- IP risk: "Regulatory requirements, government investigations and litigation can force the Company
to withdraw from, or modify its products and services for, certain countries and limit its ability to
derive value from, or enjoin others from using, its intellectual property rights. **Additionally,

they may require the Company to share its innovations with competitors.**"
- "Effective intellectual property protection is not consistently available in every country in which
the Company operates"
- Some competitors "compete primarily through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures, and by
imitating the Company's products and infringing on its intellectual property"

**Product transition / demand stimulation**
- Must continually introduce new products/services and manage **transitions**, navigate global

# AAPL - Form 10-K - Item 3 Legal Proceedings

**Source**: `filings/current/10-K.txt`, Part I, Item 3 (p. 17-18 of the 10-K)
**Fiscal Period**: FY2025 (fiscal year ended September 27, 2025)
**Extraction Date**: Shift 11
**Extracted by**: extractor_1

Apple discloses four categories of legal proceedings: (1) EU Digital Markets Act investigations, (2) a
US Department of Justice civil antitrust lawsuit, (3) the Epic Games litigation, and (4) other
ordinary-course proceedings. The two most financially material are the DMA matters (a €500M fine
already imposed plus a second investigation carrying a fine ceiling of **up to 10% of annual worldwide
net sales**, i.e. up to roughly $41.6B on FY2025 revenue) and the Epic Games injunction, which
directly attacks App Store commission economics.

The 10-Q (`AAPL_10-Q_20260627_legal_proceedings.md`) carries these forward with two material
escalations: the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to allow
Apple to charge a commission, and Apple remains under a US court order preventing it from imposing
any commission or fee on certain purchases.

### 1. EU Digital Markets Act — Article 5(4) Investigation
- **March 25, 2024**: European Commission opened a formal noncompliance investigation under
Article 5(4) of the EU DMA
- Subject matter: how developers may communicate and promote offers to end users for apps
distributed through the App Store, and how developers may conclude contracts with those end users
- **April 23, 2025**: Commission **fined the Company €500 million** and issued a **cease and desist
order** requiring Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions preventing developers from
steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store
- **Apple has appealed** the Article 5(4) decision

### 2. EU DMA — Article 6(4) Investigation
- **June 24, 2024**: Commission opened an additional formal investigation into whether Apple's new
contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces violate the DMA
- **April 23, 2025**: Commission issued **preliminary findings**
- **Financial exposure**: if the Commission makes a final determination of violation it can issue a
cease and desist order and "may impose fines up to 10% of the Company's annual worldwide net sales"
(i.e. up to ~$41.6B based on FY2025 net sales of $416,161M)
- The Commission may seek **additional fines** if it deems Apple violated a cease and desist order

- Apple's position: "The Company believes that it complies with the DMA and has continued to make
changes to its compliance plan in response to feedback and engagement with the Commission."

### 3. Department of Justice Lawsuit
- **March 21, 2024**: DOJ plus a number of state and district attorneys general filed a **civil
antitrust lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey**
- Allegations: monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for **"performance
smartphones"** and **"smartphones"** in violation of US antitrust laws
- **Relief sought: equitable relief** to redress alleged anticompetitive behaviour (note: no monetary
damages sought by DOJ in the disclosed description)
- **Additionally**, various civil litigation matters have been filed in state and federal courts in

the US alleging similar violations and **seeking monetary damages and other nonmonetary relief**
- Apple's position: "The Company believes it has substantial defenses and intends to vigorously defend
itself."

### 4. Epic Games
- **Filed**: US District Court for the Northern District of California ("California District Court"),
by Epic Games, Inc., alleging violations of federal and state antitrust laws and California's unfair
competition law based on Apple's operation of its App Store
- **2021 Injunction**: the California District Court found certain provisions of Apple's App Review
Guidelines violate California's unfair competition law and enjoined Apple from prohibiting developers
from including in their apps buttons, external links or other calls to action directing customers to
purchasing mechanisms other than Apple's in-app purchase system. Applies to apps on the **US

storefronts of the iOS and iPadOS App Stores**
- **January 16, 2024**: Apple implemented a plan to comply and filed a statement of compliance
- **September 30, 2024**: Apple filed a motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction
- **April 30, 2025**: California District Court found Apple **in violation of the 2021 Injunction**
and enjoined Apple from: (a) imposing any commission or any fee on purchases consumers make outside
an app; (b) restricting, conditioning, limiting or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to
purchases outside an app; (c) otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of
an app

- The court **denied** Apple's motion to narrow or vacate, and **referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney
for the Northern District of California to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are
appropriate** — an unusual and material escalation
- Apple appealed to the **Ninth Circuit Court**; the request to stay the decision pending appeal was
**denied**; the Ninth Circuit agreed to hear the appeal on an **expedited basis, with oral arguments
heard in October 2025**
- Apple's position: "The Company will continue to vigorously defend its actions and employees"

### 5. Other Legal Proceedings
- Various proceedings and claims arising in the ordinary course, not fully resolved
- **The Company settled certain matters during Q4 FY2025 that did not individually or in the
aggregate have a material impact on the Company's financial condition or operating results**
- Standard contingency language: outcome of litigation is inherently uncertain; resolution against
the Company for amounts above management's expectations could materially adversely affect results for
that reporting period

| Matter | Amount | Certainty | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| DMA Art. 5(4) fine (imposed 2025-04-23) | €500 million | **Determined** | Item 3 |
| DMA Art. 6(4) maximum fine | up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales (~$41.6B on FY2025 net sales) | Contingent on final determination | Item 3 |
| DMA Art. 6(4) additional fines for CDO breach | Not quantified | Contingent | Item 3 |
| DOJ civil antitrust suit | Equitable relief sought (no quantified damages disclosed) | Contingent | Item 3 |
| Other US state/federal antitrust suits | Monetary damages + nonmonetary relief, unquantified | Contingent | Item 3 |
| Epic Games injunction | Commission/fee prohibition on off-app purchases — revenue impact unquantified | In effect, under appeal | Item 3 |
| Q4 FY2025 settlements | Not material individually or in aggregate (no amount disclosed) | Resolved | Item 3 |
## Red Flags / Items for Checker

1. **The €500M DMA fine is the only quantified adverse legal determination.** No loss contingency
accrual for it is disclosed in the litigation note text. **Checker should confirm from the
Commitments and Contingencies note whether the €500M was expensed/accrued and in which period.**
2. **The DMA Art. 6(4) ceiling of 10% of worldwide net sales** is the single largest quantified
contingent exposure in the filings. It is contingent on a final determination that has not
occurred. Note that preliminary findings are not a final determination.
3. **Criminal contempt referral** in the Epic Games matter is an unusual disclosure and is not
quantified. The 10-Q shows the injunction remains operative, which directly threatens App Store

commission revenue.
4. **The DOJ seeks equitable relief only** as described — but the parallel private suits seek
monetary damages. The distinction matters for exposure modelling and should be preserved.
5. Apple discloses **no accrued loss contingency amounts** in Item 3 itself. The 10-Q Note 9
states management's opinion that "there was not at least a reasonable possibility the Company may
have incurred a material loss, or a material loss greater than a recorded accrual, concerning loss
contingencies for asserted legal and other claims." This appears to be **in tension** with the
€500M fine actually imposed and the 10%-of-sales ceiling. Flag for checker.

6. Apple states it **settled certain matters in Q4 FY2025** but gives no amount — only that they were
not material. The identity of those matters is not disclosed.

# AAPL - Form 10-K - Item 1 Business

**Source**: `filings/current/10-K.txt`, Part I, Item 1 (pp. 1-5 of the 10-K)
**Fiscal Period**: Fiscal year ended September 27, 2025 ("FY2025")
**Extraction Date**: Shift 11

Apple Inc. is a California corporation headquartered at One Apple Park Way, Cupertino, California.
It designs and sells consumer technology hardware, a portfolio of consumer software and digital
content services, and payment services. The company "designs and develops nearly the entire solution
for its products, including the hardware, operating system, numerous software applications and
related services" (Item 1, Competition). This vertical integration is a core element of the business
model: Apple captures both the device margin and the services/content margin on the installed base.

Apple manages its business **primarily on a geographic basis**, not by product line. Its reportable
segments are Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific. The company states it
has a **minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and wearables
markets** (Item 1, Competition) — a notable admission given the revenue scale.

Revenue disaggregates into **Products** and **Services**. In FY2025 Products were $307,003M and
Services $109,158M, of total net sales $416,161M, i.e. Services was 26.2% of total net sales but a
disproportionately larger share of gross profit (Services gross margin ~74% vs Products ~36.7% on
FY2025 figures derived from the income statement — see the financial metrics extraction).

Apple outsources substantially all hardware manufacturing. Note 12 states "Substantially all of the
Company's hardware products are manufactured by outsourcing partners that are located primarily in
China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam."

### Products (Item 1, Products and Services Performance Overview)
- iPhone, Mac, iPad, Wearables/Home/Accessories
- Per FY2025 disaggregated revenue (Note 2), the product line detail is captured in
`AAPL_10-K_20250927_financial_metrics.md`

### Services (Item 1)
- **Advertising**: third-party licensing arrangements and Apple's own advertising platforms
- **AppleCare**: fee-based service/support portfolio; priority technical support, access to the global
Apple authorized service network for repair/replacement, and in many cases additional coverage for
accidental damage or theft and loss, depending on country and product type
- **Cloud Services**: stores and keeps customer content up-to-date and available across multiple
Apple devices **and Windows personal computers**
- **Digital Content**: App Store and other platforms for discovery/download of apps and digital

content (books, music, video, games, podcasts); subscriptions incl. Apple Arcade, Apple Fitness+,
Apple Music, Apple News+, Apple TV (exclusive original content and live sports)
- **Payment Services**: Apple Card (co-branded credit card) and Apple Pay (cashless payment service)

### Segments (Item 1; Note 13)
Five reportable segments — Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, Rest of Asia Pacific:
- **Americas** includes both North and South America
- **Europe** includes European countries, **as well as India, the Middle East and Africa**
- **Greater China** includes China mainland, Hong Kong and Taiwan
- **Rest of Asia Pacific** includes Australia, New Zealand and Asian countries not in other segments

The company states that although segments "provide similar hardware and software products and
similar services, each one is managed separately to better align with the location of the Company's
customers and distribution partners and the unique market dynamics of each geographic region."

CODM: the Company's **CEO** is the chief operating decision maker. The CODM uses segment net sales
and operating income for pricing decisions and resource allocation for sales activities and
marketing investments. Information provided to the CODM **excludes asset information** (Note 13).

### Markets and Distribution (Item 1)
- Customers are primarily in **consumer, small and mid-sized business, education, enterprise and
government** markets
- Direct sales: retail and online stores and direct sales force, in most major markets
- Services sold through the same markets via the various service platforms
- Indirect channels: third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers
- **FY2025 channel mix: direct 40% / indirect 60% of total net sales**

### Competition (Item 1)
- Markets characterized by "aggressive price competition, downward pressure on gross margins,
continual improvement in product performance, and price sensitivity"
- Frequent new product introduction, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid
technological adoption
- **"The Company has a minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and
wearables markets, and some of the markets in which the Company competes have from time to time
experienced little to no growth or contracted overall."**

- "Competition has been particularly intense as competitors have aggressively cut prices and lowered
product margins." Some competitors can sell "at little or no profit or even at a loss."
- Principal competitive factors: price, product/service features (incl. security features), relative
price and performance, quality and reliability, design and technology innovation, a strong
third-party software and accessories ecosystem, marketing and distribution capability, service and
support, corporate reputation, and ability to effectively protect and enforce IP rights
- Company expects competition to intensify as competitors imitate Apple's approach to providing
components seamlessly within their offerings

### Supply of Components (Item 1)
- Most components generally available from multiple sources, but **certain components are currently
obtained from single or limited sources**
- Company competes for various components with other market participants; many components, even
those available from multiple sources, are at times subject to industry-wide shortage and
significant commodity pricing fluctuations
- Restrictions on international trade can increase cost or limit availability of products,
components, rare earths and other raw materials

- Apple uses some custom components not commonly used by competitors; new products often utilize
custom components available from only one source
- New technologies may create initial capacity constraints until supplier yields mature
- The company "may not be able to extend or renew agreements for the supply of components on similar
terms, or at all"
- Component suppliers "may fail, be subject to consolidation within a particular industry, or decide
to concentrate on the production of common components"

### Research and Development (Item 1)
Apple "continues to develop new technologies to enhance existing products and services, and to expand
the range of its offerings through research and development ('R&D'), licensing of intellectual
property and acquisition of third-party businesses and technology."

### Intellectual Property (Item 1)
Broad collection of IP rights: patents, designs, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets and other
forms, in the U.S. and various foreign countries. Company relies primarily on "the innovative skills,
technical competence and marketing abilities of its personnel" and regularly files patent, design,
copyright and trademark applications.

### Human Capital / Seasonality
Referenced in Item 1 with the company cautioning it "may be unable to attract or retain key
employees" (see risk extraction). Seasonality is covered in Item 7 MD&A: higher net sales in Q1
than other quarters due to seasonal holiday demand.

# AAPL - Form 10-K - Item 1 Business

**Source**: `filings/current/10-K.txt`, Part I, Item 1 (pp. 1-5 of the 10-K)
**Fiscal Period**: Fiscal year ended September 27, 2025 ("FY2025")
**Extraction Date**: Shift 11
**Extracted by**: extractor_1

Apple Inc. is a California corporation headquartered at One Apple Park Way, Cupertino, California.
It designs and sells consumer technology hardware, a portfolio of consumer software and digital
content services, and payment services. The company "designs and develops nearly the entire solution
for its products, including the hardware, operating system, numerous software applications and
related services" (Item 1, Competition). This vertical integration is a core element of the business
model: Apple captures both the device margin and the services/content margin on the installed base.

Apple manages its business **primarily on a geographic basis**, not by product line. Its reportable
segments are Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific. The company states it
has a **minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and wearables
markets** (Item 1, Competition) — a notable admission given the revenue scale.

Revenue disaggregates into **Products** and **Services**. In FY2025 Products were $307,003M and
Services $109,158M, of total net sales $416,161M, i.e. Services was 26.2% of total net sales but a
disproportionately larger share of gross profit (Services gross margin ~74% vs Products ~36.7% on
FY2025 figures derived from the income statement — see the financial metrics extraction).

Apple outsources substantially all hardware manufacturing. Note 12 states "Substantially all of the
Company's hardware products are manufactured by outsourcing partners that are located primarily in
China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam."

### Products (Item 1, Products and Services Performance Overview)
- iPhone, Mac, iPad, Wearables/Home/Accessories
- Per FY2025 disaggregated revenue (Note 2), the product line detail is captured in
`AAPL_10-K_20250927_financial_metrics.md`

### Services (Item 1)
- **Advertising**: third-party licensing arrangements and Apple's own advertising platforms
- **AppleCare**: fee-based service/support portfolio; priority technical support, access to the global
Apple authorized service network for repair/replacement, and in many cases additional coverage for
accidental damage or theft and loss, depending on country and product type
- **Cloud Services**: stores and keeps customer content up-to-date and available across multiple
Apple devices **and Windows personal computers**
- **Digital Content**: App Store and other platforms for discovery/download of apps and digital

content (books, music, video, games, podcasts); subscriptions incl. Apple Arcade, Apple Fitness+,
Apple Music, Apple News+, Apple TV (exclusive original content and live sports)
- **Payment Services**: Apple Card (co-branded credit card) and Apple Pay (cashless payment service)

### Segments (Item 1; Note 13)
Five reportable segments — Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, Rest of Asia Pacific:
- **Americas** includes both North and South America
- **Europe** includes European countries, **as well as India, the Middle East and Africa**
- **Greater China** includes China mainland, Hong Kong and Taiwan
- **Rest of Asia Pacific** includes Australia, New Zealand and Asian countries not in other segments

The company states that although segments "provide similar hardware and software products and
similar services, each one is managed separately to better align with the location of the Company's
customers and distribution partners and the unique market dynamics of each geographic region."

CODM: the Company's **CEO** is the chief operating decision maker. The CODM uses segment net sales
and operating income for pricing decisions and resource allocation for sales activities and
marketing investments. Information provided to the CODM **excludes asset information** (Note 13).

### Markets and Distribution (Item 1)
- Customers are primarily in **consumer, small and mid-sized business, education, enterprise and
government** markets
- Direct sales: retail and online stores and direct sales force, in most major markets
- Services sold through the same markets via the various service platforms
- Indirect channels: third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers
- **FY2025 channel mix: direct 40% / indirect 60% of total net sales**

### Competition (Item 1)
- Markets characterized by "aggressive price competition, downward pressure on gross margins,
continual improvement in product performance, and price sensitivity"
- Frequent new product introduction, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid
technological adoption
- **"The Company has a minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and
wearables markets, and some of the markets in which the Company competes have from time to time
experienced little to no growth or contracted overall."**

- "Competition has been particularly intense as competitors have aggressively cut prices and lowered
product margins." Some competitors can sell "at little or no profit or even at a loss."
- Principal competitive factors: price, product/service features (incl. security features), relative
price and performance, quality and reliability, design and technology innovation, a strong
third-party software and accessories ecosystem, marketing and distribution capability, service and
support, corporate reputation, and ability to effectively protect and enforce IP rights
- Company expects competition to intensify as competitors imitate Apple's approach to providing
components seamlessly within their offerings

### Supply of Components (Item 1)
- Most components generally available from multiple sources, but **certain components are currently
obtained from single or limited sources**
- Company competes for various components with other market participants; many components, even
those available from multiple sources, are at times subject to industry-wide shortage and
significant commodity pricing fluctuations
- Restrictions on international trade can increase cost or limit availability of products,
components, rare earths and other raw materials

- Apple uses some custom components not commonly used by competitors; new products often utilize
custom components available from only one source
- New technologies may create initial capacity constraints until supplier yields mature
- The company "may not be able to extend or renew agreements for the supply of components on similar
terms, or at all"
- Component suppliers "may fail, be subject to consolidation within a particular industry, or decide
to concentrate on the production of common components"

### Research and Development (Item 1)
Apple "continues to develop new technologies to enhance existing products and services, and to expand
the range of its offerings through research and development ('R&D'), licensing of intellectual
property and acquisition of third-party businesses and technology."

### Intellectual Property (Item 1)
Broad collection of IP rights: patents, designs, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets and other
forms, in the U.S. and various foreign countries. Company relies primarily on "the innovative skills,
technical competence and marketing abilities of its personnel" and regularly files patent, design,
copyright and trademark applications.

### Human Capital / Seasonality
Referenced in Item 1 with the company cautioning it "may be unable to attract or retain key
employees" (see risk extraction). Seasonality is covered in Item 7 MD&A: higher net sales in Q1
than other quarters due to seasonal holiday demand.

## Red Flags / Items for Checker

1. **Single/limited-source component dependency** is disclosed in both Item 1 and Note 12 — the
company concedes dependence it cannot hedge. Cross-reference the 10-Q statement that it is
"experiencing a period of supply constraints and increasing costs for components."
2. **Minority market share** in its four largest product markets — a structural competitive
vulnerability, disclosed by the company itself.
3. **No customer concentration disclosure** appears in the filings. Apple is not a common
concentration risk, but note that no single-customer figure is disclosed, so the checker should not
expect one.

4. **60% of net sales move through indirect channels** — less direct control over pricing,
inventory and demand signalling than a pure direct model.

# AAPL - Form 10-K - Item 1A Risk Factors

**Source**: `filings/current/10-K.txt`, Part I, Item 1A (pp. 5-15 of the 10-K)

**Extracted by**: extractor_1

Apple's risk factors run ~77,000 characters across three risk categories in the order presented:
**Macroeconomic and Industry Risks**, **Business Risks**, and **Legal and Regulatory Compliance
Risks**. Item 1A is the second-longest part of the 10-K after the financial statements, which is
itself a signal of the regulatory environment.
The three most diligence-relevant clusters for this review are:

1. **Tariffs and trade restrictions** — the single largest *named* macro risk, referencing tariffs
imposed on imports from **China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU**, plus an
active **Section 232 semiconductor investigation** by the US Department of Commerce. The company
states it "cannot predict the ultimate impact."
2. **Legal/regulatory** — 9 mentions of antitrust, 13 of regulatory, 8 of privacy, and an express
risk that legal/regulatory outcomes could require Apple to **share innovations with competitors** or
restrict its IP-derived value.
3. **Supply chain concentration** — reliance on single/limited sources and on outsourcing partners
primarily in Asia for final assembly of substantially all hardware.

Notably, **Item 1A contains no standalone data-breach or cybersecurity-incident risk heading**, no
credit-rating risk, and no reference to the EU State Aid Decision (that appears in the 10-Q tax
discussion instead).

### Category ordering in Item 1A
The three category headers appear in the filing in this sequence:
1. **Macroeconomic and Industry Risks** (first)
2. **Business Risks**
3. **Legal and Regulatory Compliance Risks** (last)
### 1. Macroeconomic and Industry Risks

**Tariffs and international trade restrictions (the dominant named risk)**
- "Restrictions on international trade, such as tariffs and other controls on imports or exports of
goods, technology or data, can materially adversely affect the Company's business and supply chain."
- "**Beginning in the second quarter of 2025, new tariffs were announced on imports to the U.S.**"
("U.S. Tariffs"), including additional tariffs on imports from **China, India, Japan, South Korea,
Taiwan, Vietnam and the European Union ("EU")**, among others
- "In response, several countries have imposed, or threatened to impose, **reciprocal tariffs** on
imports from the U.S. and other retaliatory measures"

- "Various modifications to the U.S. Tariffs have been announced and further changes could be made in
the future, which may include additional **sector-based tariffs** or other measures"
- **Section 232 investigation**: "the U.S. Department of Commerce has initiated an investigation under
**Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962**, as amended, into, among other things, imports
of **semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and their derivative products, including
downstream products that contain semiconductors**"
- "The ultimate impact remains uncertain and will depend on several factors, including whether
additional or incremental U.S. Tariffs or other measures are announced or imposed, to what extent

other countries implement tariffs or other retaliatory measures in response, and the overall
magnitude and duration of these measures."
- Escalation risk: "If disputes and conflicts further escalate, actions by governments in response
could be significantly more severe and restrictive."

**Net sales / gross margin volatility and downward pressure**
The company lists the full set of drivers of margin compression, verbatim in substance:

- Operations, retail stores and facilities in locations **prone to earthquakes and other natural

- Interruption risk from fire, power shortages, nuclear power plant accidents, industrial accidents,

issues
- Consequences: difficulty or impossibility of manufacturing and delivering products, delays and

At FY2025 year-end Apple carried **$98,657M of total debt** against **$132,420M** of cash and

**no floating-rate term debt** and **no revolving credit facility disclosed**. The only committed
short-term programme is a **commercial paper programme, proceeds of which may be used for general
corporate purposes including dividends and share repurchases** ($7,979M outstanding at year-end).

The two capital-structure items of diligence interest are: (a) the **$100B share repurchase
authorization announced in May 2025**, and (b) the **$8.8B "deemed repatriation tax payable"** under
the TCJA, which sits in other current liabilities and was still unpaid at 2025-09-27 (subsequently
paid in full in FY2026 — see the 10-Q extraction).
